chapters.title: Book 1, Chapter 1 — Subject of the First Book
paragraphs: I want to ask whether, in the civil order, there can be any sure and legitimate rule of administration — taking men as they are and laws as they might be. In this inquiry I will always try to unite what right sanctions with what is prescribed by interest, so that justice and utility are never divided.

I begin without proving the importance of the subject. People will ask whether I am a prince or a legislator, to write on politics. I answer that I am neither, and that is precisely why I do so. If I were a prince or a legislator, I would not waste time saying what needs doing — I would do it, or hold my peace.

Since I was born a citizen of a free State, and a member of the Sovereign, I feel that, however slight the influence my voice can have on public affairs, the right of voting on them makes it my duty to study them. And whenever I reflect on governments, I am happy to find that my inquiries always give me new reasons to love the one I was born under.

Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains. One man thinks himself the master of others, yet remains more enslaved than they are. How did this change come about? I do not know. What can make it legitimate? That question I think I can answer.

If I considered only force and the effects derived from it, I would say: “As long as a people is compelled to obey, and obeys, it does well; as soon as it can shake off the yoke and does so, it does still better — for in regaining its liberty by the same right that took it away, either the people is justified in taking it back, or there was no justification for those who took it in the first place.” But the social order is a sacred right that serves as the basis of every other right. This right, however, does not come from nature: it must therefore be founded on conventions. Before coming to that, I have to prove what I have just asserted.

chapters.title: Book 1, Chapter 2 — The First Societies
paragraphs: The most ancient of all societies, and the only natural one, is the family — and even there, children remain bound to the father only as long as they need him for their preservation. As soon as that need ends, the natural bond dissolves. The children, released from the obedience they owed the father, and the father, released from the care he owed his children, return equally to independence. If they remain together, they do so no longer by nature but by choice; and the family itself is then maintained only by convention.

This shared liberty is a consequence of human nature. Man’s first law is to provide for his own preservation; his first cares are those he owes himself. As soon as he reaches the age of reason, he becomes the sole judge of how best to preserve himself, and so becomes his own master.

The family, then, may be called the first model of political societies: the ruler corresponds to the father, and the people to the children. And all, being born free and equal, give up their liberty only for their own advantage. The only difference is that, within a family, a father’s love for his children repays him for the care he takes of them, whereas in the State the pleasure of commanding takes the place of the love a chief cannot feel for the peoples under him.

Grotius denies that all human power is established for the benefit of the governed, and cites slavery as his example. His standard method of argument is to establish right from fact.[1] One could use a more logical method, but none more flattering to tyrants.

According to Grotius, then, it is an open question whether the human race belongs to a hundred men, or those hundred men to the human race; and throughout his book, he seems to incline toward the first view — which is also Hobbes’s. On this account, the human species is divided into so many herds of cattle, each with a ruler who guards them only in order to devour them.

Just as a shepherd is of a higher nature than his flock, so the shepherds of men — that is, their rulers — are of a higher nature than the peoples under them. This, Philo tells us, was the Emperor Caligula’s reasoning, from which he concluded, equally well, either that kings were gods or that men were beasts.
Caligula’s reasoning agrees with Hobbes’s and Grotius’s. Aristotle, before any of them, had said that men are by no means equal by nature: some are born for slavery, others for dominion.

Aristotle was right, but he mistook the effect for the cause. Nothing is more certain than that every man born in slavery is born for slavery. Slaves lose everything in their chains, even the desire to escape them: they come to love their servitude, just as the comrades of Ulysses loved their brutish condition.[2] If, then, there are slaves by nature, it is only because there have first been slaves against nature. Force made the first slaves, and their cowardice has kept them so.

I have said nothing of King Adam, or of Emperor Noah, father of the three great monarchs who divided up the universe — like the children of Saturn, whom some scholars have recognized in them. I trust I will be properly thanked for my modesty; for, as a direct descendant of one of these princes — perhaps even of the eldest branch — who knows whether a careful check of titles might not leave me the legitimate king of the human race? In any case, there is no doubt that Adam was sovereign of the world, just as Robinson Crusoe was of his island, as long as he was its only inhabitant; and this empire had the advantage that the monarch, safe on his throne, had no rebellions, wars, or conspirators to fear.

chapters.title: Book 1, Chapter 3 — The Right of the Strongest
paragraphs: The strongest is never strong enough to be master forever, unless he turns his strength into right and obedience into duty. Hence the so-called right of the strongest — a phrase that seems ironic, but is in fact laid down as a fundamental principle. Yet are we never to have an explanation of it? Force is a physical power; I cannot see what moral effect it can possibly produce. To yield to force is an act of necessity, not of will — at most, an act of prudence. In what sense can it be a duty?

Suppose for a moment that this so-called “right” exists. The only result, I claim, is a heap of inexplicable nonsense. For if force creates right, the effect changes with the cause: every greater force inherits the right of the lesser. As soon as one can disobey with impunity, disobedience is legitimate; and since the strongest is always in the right, the only thing that matters is to act so as to become the strongest. But what kind of right is it that perishes when force fails? If we must obey because we are forced, there is no need to obey because we ought; and if we are not forced to obey, we have no obligation to do so. Clearly, the word “right” adds nothing to force: in this connection, it means absolutely nothing.

“Obey the powers that be.” If this means “yield to force,” it is a sound but pointless rule: I can guarantee it will never be broken. All power comes from God, I grant; but so does every disease — does that mean we are forbidden to call the doctor? A robber surprises me at the edge of a wood: must I not only hand over my purse under compulsion, but, even if I could keep it, am I bound in conscience to give it up? After all, the pistol he holds is also a power.
Let us, then, accept that force does not create right, and that we are obliged to obey only legitimate powers. In that case, my original question returns.

chapters.title: Book 1, Chapter 4 — Slavery
paragraphs: Since no man has natural authority over his fellow, and since force creates no right, we must conclude that conventions are the basis of all legitimate authority among men.

If an individual, says Grotius, can alienate his liberty and make himself a master’s slave, why could not a whole people do the same and submit itself to a king? This passage contains many ambiguous words that would need explaining; but let us limit ourselves to the word _alienate_. To alienate is to give or to sell. Now, a man who becomes another’s slave does not give himself away — he sells himself, at the very least for his subsistence. But what does a people sell itself for? Far from supplying his subjects with their subsistence, a king draws his own only from them; and, as Rabelais reminds us, kings do not live on nothing. Do subjects, then, give over their persons on the condition that the king will also take their property? I cannot see what they have left to preserve.

It will be said that the despot guarantees his subjects civil peace. Granted — but what do they gain, if the wars his ambition brings down on them, his insatiable greed, and the harassment of his ministers weigh more heavily on them than their own quarrels would have done? What do they gain, if the very tranquility they enjoy is itself one of their miseries? Tranquility is also found in dungeons; but is that enough to make them desirable places to live? The Greeks imprisoned in the Cyclops’s cave lived very tranquilly there, while they waited their turn to be devoured.

To say that a man gives himself away for nothing is to say something absurd and unthinkable. Such an act is null and illegitimate, by the very fact that the man performing it is out of his mind. To say the same of an entire people is to imagine a people of madmen — and madness creates no right.

Even if each man could alienate himself, he could not alienate his children: they are born men, and free; their liberty belongs to them, and no one but they has the right to dispose of it. Before they reach the age of reason, the father can lay down conditions in their name for their preservation and well-being, but he cannot give them away irrevocably and without conditions. Such a gift goes against the ends of nature and exceeds the rights of paternity. To legitimize an arbitrary government, then, the people would have to be in a position, in every generation, to accept or reject it; but if that were the case, the government would no longer be arbitrary.

To renounce one’s liberty is to renounce being a man, to surrender the rights of humanity and even its duties. For someone who renounces everything, no compensation is possible. Such a renunciation is incompatible with man’s nature; to strip his will of all liberty is to strip his actions of all morality. Finally, it is an empty and self-contradictory convention that establishes, on one side, absolute authority, and, on the other, unlimited obedience. Is it not clear that we can owe no obligation to a person from whom we have the right to demand everything? Does this condition alone — without equivalence or exchange — not in itself nullify the act? For what right can my slave have against me, when everything he has belongs to me, and, his right being mine, this right of mine against myself is a phrase devoid of meaning?

Grotius and others find another origin for the so-called right of slavery: war. Since the victor, on their view, has the right to kill the vanquished, the latter can buy back his life at the price of his liberty — and they hold this convention all the more legitimate because it benefits both parties.

But it is clear that this supposed right to kill the conquered cannot be deduced from the state of war at all. Men, by the simple fact that, while they live in their primitive independence, they have no relations stable enough to constitute either peace or war, cannot be natural enemies. War is constituted by a relation between things, not between persons; and since the state of war cannot arise out of merely personal relations, but only out of real ones, private war — war of man against man — can exist neither in the state of nature, where there is no settled property, nor in the social state, where everything is under the authority of the laws.

Individual fights, duels, and brawls are acts that cannot constitute a state. As for the private wars authorized by the Establishments of Louis IX, King of France, and suspended by the Peace of God — these are abuses of feudalism, a system that was absurd if any ever was, and contrary to both natural right and any sound polity.

War, then, is a relation not between man and man, but between State and State, in which individuals are enemies only incidentally — not as men, nor even as citizens,[1] but as soldiers; not as members of their country, but as its defenders. In the end, each State can have for enemies only other States, and not men; for between things of differing nature there can be no real relation.

Moreover, this principle agrees with the established rules of every age and the constant practice of all civilized peoples. Declarations of war are notifications less to powers than to their subjects. The foreigner — whether king, individual, or people — who robs, kills, or detains subjects without declaring war on the prince is not an enemy but a brigand. Even in real war, a just prince, while seizing in the enemy country everything that belongs to the public, respects the lives and goods of individuals: he respects the rights on which his own are founded. The aim of war being the destruction of the hostile State, the other side has the right to kill its defenders so long as they are bearing arms; but as soon as they lay them down and surrender, they cease to be enemies, or instruments of the enemy, and become once again merely men, whose lives no one has any right to take. Sometimes it is even possible to kill the State without killing a single one of its members; and war confers no right that is not necessary to its own purpose. These principles are not those of Grotius: they are not founded on the authority of poets, but drawn from the nature of reality and grounded in reason.

The right of conquest has no foundation other than the right of the strongest. If war does not give the conqueror the right to slaughter the conquered peoples, the right to enslave them cannot be based on a right that does not exist. No one has the right to kill an enemy except when he cannot make him a slave, and so the right to enslave him cannot be derived from the right to kill him. It is therefore an unfair exchange to make him buy at the price of his liberty a life over which the victor has no right. Is it not obvious that there is a vicious circle in founding the right of life and death on the right of slavery, and the right of slavery on the right of life and death?

Even if we grant this terrible right to kill everyone, I maintain that a slave taken in war, or a conquered people, is under no obligation to a master except to obey him as far as he is compelled to do so. By taking an equivalent for his life, the victor has not done him a favor; instead of killing him uselessly, he has killed him usefully. Far from gaining over him any authority beyond that of force, the state of war between them continues to exist: their mutual relation is the effect of it, and the use of the right of war implies no treaty of peace. A convention has indeed been made; but this convention, far from ending the state of war, presupposes its continuation.

So, from whatever angle we examine the question, the right of slavery is null and void, not only as illegitimate but as absurd and meaningless. The words _slave_ and _right_ contradict each other; they are mutually exclusive. It will always be equally foolish for a man to say to another man, or to a people: “I am making with you a convention entirely at your expense and entirely to my advantage; I shall keep it as long as I like, and you shall keep it as long as I like.”

I know that the siege of Clusium and other isolated incidents can be cited against me; but I am citing laws and customs. The Romans are the people who least often violated their laws — and no other people has had such good ones.

chapters.title: Book 1, Chapter 5 — That We Must Always Go Back to a First Convention
paragraphs: Even if I granted everything I have just been refuting, the friends of despotism would gain nothing by it. There will always be a vast difference between subduing a multitude and ruling a society. Even if scattered individuals were enslaved one after another by a single man, however numerous they might be, I still see only a master and his slaves — certainly not a people and its ruler. I see what might be called an aggregation, but not an association; there is, as yet, neither public good nor body politic. The man in question, even if he has enslaved half the world, is still only an individual; his interest, separated from that of others, remains a purely private interest. If this same man dies, his empire is left scattered behind him, without unity, just as an oak collapses into a heap of ashes when the fire has consumed it.

A people, says Grotius, can give itself to a king. So according to Grotius, a people is a people before it gives itself. The gift is itself a civil act, and presupposes public deliberation. It would therefore be better, before examining the act by which a people gives itself to a king, to examine the act by which it has become a people in the first place; for this prior act, being necessarily earlier than the other, is the true foundation of society.

Indeed, if there were no prior convention, where — unless the election were unanimous — would the obligation come from for the minority to submit to the majority’s choice? By what right do a hundred men who want a master vote on behalf of ten who do not? The rule of majority voting is itself something established by convention, and presupposes unanimity, at least once.

chapters.title: Book 1, Chapter 6 — The Social Compact
paragraphs: Suppose men have reached the point where the obstacles to their preservation in the state of nature outweigh, by their resistance, the resources each individual has at his disposal to maintain himself in that state. That primitive condition can no longer continue; the human race would perish if it did not change its way of existence.

But since men cannot generate new forces, only unite and direct existing ones, the only way they can preserve themselves is by forming, through aggregation, a sum of forces great enough to overcome the resistance — forces that they then bring into play through a single motive power and make act in concert.

This sum of forces can arise only from the coming together of several persons. But since each man’s force and liberty are the chief instruments of his preservation, how can he commit them without harming his own interests, or neglecting the care he owes himself? This difficulty, as it bears on my present subject, can be stated in the following terms:

“The problem is to find a form of association that will defend and protect, with the whole common force, the person and goods of every associate, and in which each, while uniting himself with all, may yet obey only himself, and remain as free as before.” This is the fundamental problem to which the _Social Contract_ provides the solution.

The clauses of this contract are so determined by the very nature of the act that the slightest modification would render them empty and ineffective; so that, although they have perhaps never been formally set forth, they are everywhere the same and everywhere tacitly accepted and recognized — until, when the social compact is violated, each person regains his original rights and resumes his natural liberty, while losing the conventional liberty for which he had renounced it.

These clauses, properly understood, can be reduced to one: the total alienation of each associate, with all his rights, to the whole community. For, in the first place, since each gives himself absolutely, the conditions are the same for everyone; and, this being so, no one has any interest in making them burdensome to others.

Moreover, since the alienation is without reservation, the union is as perfect as it can be, and no associate has anything more to demand. For if individuals retained certain rights — there being no common superior to decide between them and the public — each, being his own judge on one point, would soon claim to be so on every point; the state of nature would persist, and the association would necessarily become either inoperative or tyrannical.

Finally, in giving himself to all, each man gives himself to no one; and since there is no associate over whom he does not gain the same right as he yields others over himself, he gains an equivalent for everything he loses, and an increase of force for the preservation of what he has.
If, then, we strip away from the social compact what is not essential to it, we find it reduces to these terms:
_“Each of us puts his person and all his power in common under the supreme direction of the general will; and in our corporate capacity, we receive each member as an indivisible part of the whole.”_

At once, in place of the individual personality of each contracting party, this act of association creates a moral and collective body, made up of as many members as the assembly contains votes, and receiving from this very act its unity, its common identity, its life, and its will. This public person, formed by the union of all the others, used to be called a _city_,[1] and is now called a _Republic_ or _body politic_; its members call it _State_ when it is passive, _Sovereign_ when it is active, and _Power_ when comparing it with others like itself. Those associated within it are collectively called _the people_, and individually _citizens_, insofar as they share in the sovereign power, and _subjects_, insofar as they are under the laws of the State. But these terms are often confused and used interchangeably; it is enough to know how to distinguish them when they are used precisely.

The Carthaginians long ago paid dearly for this same mistake. I have never read of the title of citizen being given to the subjects of any prince — not even the ancient Macedonians, nor the English of today, though they are nearer to liberty than anyone else. The French alone everywhere casually adopt the name of citizens, because, as their dictionaries show, they have no idea what it means; otherwise they would, in usurping it, be guilty of the crime of _lèse-majesté_. Among them, the name expresses a virtue, not a right. When Bodin spoke of our citizens and townsmen, he made a serious blunder by mistaking the one for the other. M. d’Alembert avoided the error: in his article on Geneva, he clearly distinguished the four orders of men (or even five, counting mere foreigners) who live in our town, of which only two compose the Republic. No other French writer, to my knowledge, has grasped the real meaning of the word citizen.

chapters.title: Book 1, Chapter 7 — The Sovereign
paragraphs: This formula shows us that the act of association involves a mutual undertaking between the public and the individuals, and that each individual, in making, so to speak, a contract with himself, is bound in two capacities: as a member of the Sovereign he is bound to the individuals, and as a member of the State he is bound to the Sovereign. But the maxim of civil right that no one is bound by undertakings made to himself does not apply here; for there is a great difference between incurring an obligation toward yourself and incurring one toward a whole of which you are a part.

Note further that public deliberation, while competent to bind every subject to the Sovereign — because of the two different capacities in which each may be regarded — cannot, for the opposite reason, bind the Sovereign to itself; and that it is consequently against the nature of the body politic for the Sovereign to impose on itself a law it cannot break. Since it can regard itself in only one capacity, it is in the position of an individual contracting with himself; from which it is clear that no fundamental law of any kind can be binding on the body of the people — not even the social contract itself. This does not mean that the body politic cannot enter into undertakings with others, provided the contract is not violated by them; for in relation to anything outside it, it becomes a simple being, an individual.

But the body politic, or the Sovereign, drawing its whole being from the sanctity of the contract, can never bind itself, even toward an outsider, to anything that derogates from the original act — for example, to alienate any part of itself, or to submit to another Sovereign. Violating the act by which it exists would be self-annihilation, and what is itself nothing can create nothing.

As soon as this multitude is so united into one body, it is impossible to harm one of the members without attacking the body, and still less to harm the body without the members feeling it. Duty and interest therefore equally oblige the two contracting parties to help each other; and the same men should seek to combine, in their double capacity, all the advantages that depend on it.

Again, the Sovereign, being made up entirely of the individuals who compose it, neither has nor can have any interest contrary to theirs; and therefore the sovereign power needs to give no guarantee to its subjects, since it is impossible for the body to wish to harm all its members. We shall see later that it cannot harm any of them in particular either. The Sovereign, simply by virtue of what it is, is always what it should be.

It is not the same, however, with the relation of the subjects to the Sovereign, which, despite the common interest, would have no security that the subjects will fulfill their undertakings unless it found a way to assure itself of their loyalty.

In fact, each individual, as a man, may have a particular will contrary or different from the general will he has as a citizen. His private interest may speak to him quite differently from the common interest; his absolute and naturally independent existence may make him regard what he owes to the common cause as a free contribution, the loss of which will harm others less than its payment burdens him. Treating the moral person that constitutes the State as a persona ficta — because it is not a man — he may wish to enjoy the rights of citizenship without being willing to fulfill the duties of a subject. Allowing such an injustice to continue would be the ruin of the body politic.

So, in order that the social compact not be an empty formula, it tacitly includes the undertaking — the only one that can give force to all the rest — that whoever refuses to obey the general will shall be compelled to do so by the whole body. This means nothing less than that he shall be forced to be free; for this is the condition that, by giving each citizen to his country, secures him against all personal dependence. In this lies the key to the working of the political machine; this alone makes civil undertakings legitimate, which without it would be absurd, tyrannical, and open to the most frightful abuses.

chapters.title: Book 1, Chapter 8 — The Civil State
paragraphs: The passage from the state of nature to the civil state produces a remarkable change in man, by replacing instinct with justice in his conduct, and giving his actions the morality they had previously lacked. Only then, when the voice of duty replaces physical impulse, and right replaces appetite, does _man_ — who until then had considered only himself — find that he is forced to act on different principles, and to consult his reason before listening to his inclinations. Although in this state he gives up some advantages he had from nature, he gains in return others so great — his faculties so stirred and developed, his ideas so widened, his feelings so ennobled, his whole soul so uplifted — that, if the abuses of this new condition did not so often degrade him below the one he left, he would be bound to bless continually the happy moment that took him from it forever, and turned him from a stupid, unimaginative animal into an intelligent being and a man.

Let us draw up the whole account in commensurable terms. What man loses by the social contract is his natural liberty and an unlimited right to everything he tries for and manages to get; what he gains is civil liberty and ownership of all he possesses. To weigh one against the other without confusion, we must clearly distinguish natural liberty, which is bounded only by the strength of the individual, from civil liberty, which is limited by the general will; and possession, which is merely the effect of force or the right of the first occupier, from property, which can be founded only on a positive title.

Beyond all this, we could add to what man acquires in the civil state moral liberty, which alone makes him truly master of himself; for the mere impulse of appetite is slavery, while obedience to a law we prescribe to ourselves is liberty. But I have already said enough on this point, and the philosophical meaning of the word liberty does not concern us here.

chapters.title: Book 1, Chapter 9 — Real Property
paragraphs: Each member of the community gives himself to it, at the moment of its founding, just as he is, with all the resources at his command, including the goods he possesses. This act does not change the nature of possession when it changes hands; it does not become property in the hands of the Sovereign. But because the forces of the city are incomparably greater than those of an individual, public possession is in fact stronger and more irrevocable, without being any more legitimate — at any rate from the point of view of foreigners. For the State, in relation to its members, is master of all their goods through the social contract, which within the State is the basis of every right; but in relation to other powers, it is master only by the right of the first occupier, which it derives from its members.

The right of the first occupier, though more real than the right of the strongest, only becomes a real right once the right of property has already been established. Every man naturally has a right to everything he needs; but the positive act that makes him owner of one thing excludes him from everything else. Having his share, he must keep to it, and can have no further claim against the community. This is why the right of the first occupier, so weak in the state of nature, commands the respect of every man in civil society. In this right, what we are respecting is not so much what belongs to another as what does not belong to ourselves.

In general, to establish the right of the first occupier over a plot of ground, the following conditions must be met: first, the land must not yet be inhabited; second, a man must occupy only the amount he needs for his subsistence; and third, possession must be taken not by an empty ceremony but by labor and cultivation — the only sign of ownership that should be respected by others, in the absence of a legal title.

In granting the right of first occupancy to necessity and labor, are we not really stretching it as far as it can go? Can such a right be left unlimited? Is it enough to set foot on a plot of common ground to claim instantly to be its master? Is it enough that a man has the strength to drive others off for a moment to establish his right to keep them away forever? How can a man or a people seize an immense territory and shut it off from the rest of the world, except by a punishable usurpation, since by such an act all others are robbed of the dwelling place and the means of subsistence that nature gave them in common? When Nuñez Balbao, standing on the seashore, took possession of the South Seas and the whole of South America in the name of the crown of Castile, was that enough to dispossess all their actual inhabitants and shut them out from every prince of the world? On that reasoning, these ceremonies are pointlessly multiplied, and the Catholic King need only take possession all at once, from his apartment, of the whole universe — making a subsequent reservation only for whatever was already in the possession of other princes.

We can imagine how the lands of individuals, where they were contiguous and came to be united, became public territory, and how the right of Sovereignty, extending from the subjects to the lands they held, became at once real and personal. Owners were thereby made more dependent, and the forces at their command were used to guarantee their loyalty. The advantage of this seems not to have been felt by ancient monarchs, who called themselves King of the Persians, Scythians, or Macedonians, and seem to have regarded themselves more as rulers of men than masters of a country. Today’s monarchs are more clever: they call themselves King of France, Spain, England, and so on; holding the land, they are quite confident of holding the inhabitants.

The peculiar thing about this alienation is that, in taking over the goods of individuals, the community, far from despoiling them, only assures them legitimate possession, turning usurpation into a true right and enjoyment into ownership. The owners, regarded as trustees of the public good, with their rights respected by every member of the State and defended against foreign aggression by all its forces, have, through a cession that benefits both the public and themselves still more, in a sense gained back everything they gave up. This paradox is easily explained by the distinction between the rights the Sovereign and the owner have over the same estate, as we shall see later. It may also happen that men begin to unite with one another before they own anything, and that, later occupying a tract of country sufficient for all, they enjoy it in common, or share it out among themselves — equally, or on a scale fixed by the Sovereign. However the acquisition is made, each individual’s right to his own estate is always subordinate to the right the community has over all; without this, there would be neither stability in the social bond nor real force in the exercise of Sovereignty.

I shall end this chapter and this book by remarking on a fact on which the whole social system should rest: namely, that, far from destroying natural inequality, the fundamental compact substitutes a moral and legitimate equality for whatever physical inequality nature may have set up among men, and that men, who may be unequal in strength or intelligence, all become equal by convention and by legal right.[1]

chapters.title: Book 2, Chapter 1 — That Sovereignty Is Inalienable
paragraphs: The first and most important conclusion to draw from the principles laid down so far is that the general will alone can direct the State toward the purpose for which it was instituted — namely, the common good. For if the clash of particular interests made the establishment of societies necessary, the agreement of those same interests made it possible. What is common to these different interests is what forms the social bond; and if there were no point of agreement among them all, no society could exist. It is solely on the basis of this common interest that every society should be governed.

I therefore hold that Sovereignty, being nothing other than the exercise of the general will, can never be alienated, and that the Sovereign, who is nothing but a collective being, can be represented only by himself. Power can indeed be transmitted, but not will.

In reality, while it is not impossible for a particular will to coincide with the general will on some point, it is at least impossible for the agreement to be lasting and constant; for the particular will tends, by its very nature, toward partiality, while the general will tends toward equality. It is even more impossible to have any guarantee of this agreement; for even if it always existed, it would be the effect not of art but of chance. The Sovereign may indeed say: “I now actually will what this man wills, or at least what he says he wills”; but it cannot say: “What he wills tomorrow, I shall also will” — for it is absurd for the will to bind itself for the future, and no will is required to consent to anything that is not for the good of the being who wills. So if the people simply promises to obey, by that very act it dissolves itself and loses what makes it a people; the moment a master exists, there is no longer a Sovereign, and from that moment the body politic has ceased to exist.

This does not mean that the rulers’ commands cannot pass for general wills, so long as the Sovereign, free to oppose them, raises no opposition. In such a case, universal silence is taken to imply the consent of the people. This will be explained later.

chapters.title: Book 2, Chapter 2 — That Sovereignty Is Indivisible
paragraphs: Sovereignty is indivisible for the same reason it is inalienable; for a will is either general or it is not.[1] It is the will either of the body of the people, or of only a part of it. In the first case, the will, when declared, is an act of Sovereignty and constitutes law; in the second, it is merely a particular will, or an act of magistracy — at most a decree.

But our political theorists, unable to divide Sovereignty in principle, divide it according to its object: into force and will; into legislative and executive power; into rights of taxation, justice, and war; into internal administration and the power to make foreign treaties. Sometimes they jumble these sections together, sometimes they distinguish them; they turn the Sovereign into a fantastical being made of various pieces stitched together — as though they were assembling a man out of several bodies, one with eyes, another with arms, another with feet, and each with nothing else. We are told that the jugglers of Japan dismember a child in front of the audience, then throw the limbs into the air one after another, and the child falls down alive and whole. Our political theorists’ tricks are very much like that: they first dismember the body politic by an illusion worthy of a fairground, and then put it back together again — we know not how.

This error comes from a lack of precise notions about Sovereign authority, and from taking for parts of it what are only emanations from it. So, for example, the acts of declaring war and making peace have been regarded as acts of Sovereignty; but this is not the case, since these acts do not constitute law but only apply it — they are particular acts deciding how the law applies, as will be clear once the idea attached to the word _law_ has been defined.

If we examined the other divisions in the same way, we would find that whenever Sovereignty seems to be divided, it is an illusion: the rights taken to be part of Sovereignty are really all subordinate to it, and always presuppose supreme wills whose execution they merely sanction.

It would be impossible to estimate how much obscurity this lack of precision has cast over the rulings of writers on political right when, working from the principles they have laid down, they pass judgment on the respective rights of kings and peoples. Anyone can see, in Chapters III and IV of the First Book of Grotius, how the learned man and his translator, Barbeyrac, tangle and tie themselves up in their own sophistries — afraid of saying too little or too much of what they think, and so offending the interests they have to placate. Grotius, a refugee in France, dissatisfied with his own country and eager to flatter Louis XIII, to whom his book is dedicated, spares no effort to strip the people of all their rights and to invest kings with them by every conceivable artifice. This would also have suited Barbeyrac, who dedicated his translation to George I of England. Unfortunately, the expulsion of James II — which he called his “abdication” — forced him to use every reserve, to dodge and equivocate, in order to avoid making William out to be a usurper. If these two writers had adopted the true principles, all the difficulties would have vanished and they could have been consistent throughout. But this would have been a sad truth for them to tell, and would have flattered no one but the people. Truth, however, is no road to fortune, and the people hands out neither ambassadorships, nor professorships, nor pensions.

chapters.title: Book 2, Chapter 3 — Whether the General Will Is Fallible
paragraphs: It follows from what has gone before that the general will is always right and tends toward the public good; but it does not follow that the deliberations of the people are always equally correct. Our will is always for our own good, but we do not always see what that good is; the people is never corrupted, but it is often deceived, and only on such occasions does it appear to will what is bad.

There is often a great deal of difference between the will of all and the general will. The general will considers only the common interest, while the will of all takes private interests into account, and is no more than the sum of particular wills. But strip from those particular wills the pluses and minuses that cancel each other,[1] and what is left as the sum of the differences is the general will.

If, when the people deliberated with adequate information, the citizens had no communication with one another, the grand total of the small differences would always give the general will, and the decision would always be a good one. But when factions arise, and partial associations form within the great association, the will of each of these smaller associations becomes general in relation to its own members, while remaining particular in relation to the State. We may then say there are no longer as many votes as there are men, but only as many as there are associations. The differences become fewer and yield a less general result. Finally, when one of these associations becomes so large that it prevails over all the rest, the result is no longer a sum of small differences but a single difference; in that case, there is no general will any more, and the prevailing opinion is purely particular.

It is therefore essential, if the general will is to express itself, that there be no partial society within the State, and that each citizen think only his own thoughts:[2] which was indeed the sublime and unique system established by the great Lycurgus. But if there are partial societies, it is best to have as many as possible, and to keep them from becoming unequal — as Solon, Numa, and Servius did. These are the only precautions that can guarantee that the general will shall always be enlightened, and that the people shall in no way deceive itself.

chapters.title: Book 2, Chapter 4 — The Limits of the Sovereign Power
paragraphs: If the State is a moral person whose life consists in the union of its members, and if its most important concern is its own preservation, it must possess a universal and compelling force, in order to move and arrange each part as is most advantageous to the whole. Just as nature gives every man absolute power over his own limbs, so the social compact gives the body politic absolute power over all its members; and it is this power, under the direction of the general will, that bears, as I have said, the name of Sovereignty.

But besides the public person, we must also consider the private persons composing it, whose life and liberty are naturally independent of it. We are bound, then, to distinguish clearly between the respective rights of the citizens and of the Sovereign,[1] and between the duties the former must fulfill as subjects, and the natural rights they ought to enjoy as men.

I admit that, by the social compact, each man alienates only such part of his powers, goods, and liberty as it is important for the community to control; but it must also be granted that the Sovereign alone is judge of what is important.

Every service a citizen can render the State, he ought to render as soon as the Sovereign demands it; but the Sovereign, for its part, cannot impose any chains on its subjects that are useless to the community — and indeed cannot even wish to do so, for nothing can occur without a cause, by the law of reason any more than by the law of nature.

The undertakings that bind us to the social body are obligatory only because they are mutual; and their nature is such that, in fulfilling them, we cannot work for others without working for ourselves. Why is the general will always in the right, and why do all continually will the happiness of each, unless it is because there is not a man who does not think of “each” as meaning himself, and consider himself when voting for all? This proves that the equality of rights, and the idea of justice that such equality creates, originate in the preference each man gives himself, and so in the very nature of man. It proves that the general will, to be truly such, must be general in its object as well as in its essence; that it must come from all and apply to all; and that it loses its natural rectitude when it is directed to some particular and determinate object — for in that case, we are judging of something foreign to us, and have no true principle of fairness to guide us.

Indeed, as soon as a question of particular fact or right arises on a point not previously settled by a general convention, the matter becomes contentious. It is a case in which the individuals concerned are one party and the public the other, but in which I see neither the law that ought to be followed nor the judge who ought to give the decision. In such a case, it would be absurd to refer the question to an express decision of the general will, which can only be the conclusion reached by one of the parties — and so will be, for the other party, merely an external and particular will, in this case inclined to injustice and prone to error. Just as a particular will cannot stand for the general will, so the general will, in turn, changes its nature when its object is particular, and, as general, cannot pronounce on a particular man or a particular fact. When, for example, the people of Athens nominated or removed its rulers, decreed honors for one and imposed penalties on another, and, by a multitude of particular decrees, indiscriminately exercised all the functions of government, in such cases it no longer had a general will in the strict sense; it was acting no longer as Sovereign, but as magistrate. This will seem contrary to current views, but I must be allowed time to set out my own.

From the foregoing, it should be clear that what makes the will general is less the number of voters than the common interest uniting them; for under this system, each necessarily submits to the conditions he imposes on others. This admirable agreement between interest and justice gives common deliberations a fairness that vanishes the instant any particular question is discussed, in the absence of a common interest to unite and identify the ruling of the judge with that of the party.

From whatever angle we approach our principle, we reach the same conclusion: the social compact establishes among the citizens an equality such that they all bind themselves to observe the same conditions, and so should all enjoy the same rights. Thus, by the very nature of the compact, every “act of Sovereignty” — that is, every authentic act of the general will — binds or favors all the citizens equally; the Sovereign recognizes only the body of the nation, and draws no distinctions between those of whom it is composed. What, then, strictly speaking, is an act of Sovereignty? It is not a convention between a superior and an inferior, but a convention between the body and each of its members. It is legitimate, because based on the social contract; equitable, because common to all; useful, because it can have no other object than the general good; and stable, because guaranteed by the public force and the supreme power. As long as the subjects have to submit only to conventions of this sort, they obey no one but their own will; and to ask how far the respective rights of the Sovereign and the citizens extend is to ask up to what point the citizens can enter into undertakings with themselves — each with all, and all with each.

We can see from this that the sovereign power, absolute, sacred, and inviolable as it is, neither does nor can exceed the limits of general conventions, and that every man may dispose at will of whatever goods and liberty those conventions leave him; so that the Sovereign never has the right to lay more burdens on one subject than on another, since in that case the question becomes particular and ceases to fall within its competence.

Once these distinctions are admitted, it becomes so untrue that there is, in the social contract, any real renunciation on the part of the individuals, that the position they find themselves in as a result of the contract is actually preferable to the one they had before. Instead of a renunciation, they have made an advantageous exchange: instead of an uncertain and precarious way of living, they have got a better and more secure one; instead of natural independence, they have got liberty; instead of the power to harm others, security for themselves; and instead of their own strength, which others might overcome, a right that the social union makes invincible. Their very life, which they have devoted to the State, is constantly protected by it; and when they risk it in the State’s defense, what more are they doing than giving back what they have received from it? What are they doing that they would not do more often, and at greater peril, in the state of nature, where they would inevitably have to fight for their lives in defense of what is the means of their preservation? All must indeed fight when their country needs them; but then no one ever has to fight for himself alone. Are we not gaining something by running, on behalf of what gives us our security, only some of the risks we would have to run for ourselves the moment we lost it?

chapters.title: Book 2, Chapter 5 — The Right of Life and Death
paragraphs: It is often asked how individuals, having no right to dispose of their own lives, can transfer to the Sovereign a right they do not themselves possess. The difficulty here, it seems to me, lies in the way the question is put. Every man has the right to risk his own life in order to preserve it. Has anyone ever called the man who throws himself out a window to escape a fire a suicide? Has such a charge ever been brought against the man who perishes in a storm because, when he went on board, he knew of the danger?

The aim of the social treaty is the preservation of the contracting parties. Whoever wills the end wills the means as well, and those means must involve some risks, even some losses. Whoever wishes to preserve his life at the expense of others should also, when necessary, be ready to give it up for them. Furthermore, the citizen is no longer the judge of the dangers to which the law calls on him to expose himself; and when the prince says to him: “It is expedient for the State that you should die,” he ought to die — because it is only on that condition that he has lived in security up to that moment, and because his life is no longer simply nature’s gift, but a conditional gift from the State.

The death penalty inflicted on criminals can be looked at in much the same light. We agree to die if we ourselves turn assassin, in order that we may not fall victim to one. Far from disposing of our own lives in this treaty, we are thinking only of safeguarding them, and we cannot suppose that any of the parties expects, at the time, to end up hanged.

Again, every wrongdoer, by attacking social rights, becomes through his offense a rebel and a traitor to his country; in violating its laws, he ceases to be a member of it; he even makes war against it. In such a case, the preservation of the State is incompatible with his own, and one or the other must perish; in putting the guilty man to death, we are killing not so much the citizen as an enemy. The trial and judgment are the proof that he has broken the social treaty, and is therefore no longer a member of the State. Since he has acknowledged himself as such by living there, he must be removed — by exile, as a violator of the compact, or by death, as a public enemy. For such an enemy is no longer a moral person, but merely a man; and in such a case, the right of war is to kill the vanquished.

But, it will be said, the condemnation of a criminal is a particular act. I admit it. But such condemnation is not a function of the Sovereign; it is a right the Sovereign can confer without being able to exercise itself. All my ideas hang together, but I cannot lay them all out at once.

We may add that frequent punishments are always a sign of weakness or laziness on the part of the government. There is not a single wrongdoer who could not be turned to some good. The State has no right to put to death, even as an example, anyone whom it can leave alive without danger.

The right of pardoning, or exempting the guilty from a penalty imposed by the law and pronounced by the judge, belongs only to the authority that is superior to both judge and law — namely, the Sovereign. Even the Sovereign’s right in this matter is far from clear, and the cases for exercising it are extremely rare. In a well-governed State there are few punishments, not because there are many pardons, but because criminals are rare; it is when a State is in decay that the multitude of crimes guarantees impunity. Under the Roman Republic, neither the Senate nor the Consuls ever attempted to pardon; even the people never did, though it sometimes revoked its own decision. Frequent pardons mean that crime will soon no longer need them, and anyone can see where that leads. But I feel my heart protesting and holding back my pen; let us leave such questions to the just man who has never offended, and who would himself stand in no need of pardon.

chapters.title: Book 2, Chapter 6 — Law
paragraphs: By the social compact we have given the body politic existence and life; we now have to give it movement and will, through legislation. For the original act by which the body is formed and united still does nothing to determine what it ought to do for its preservation.

What is good and in conformity with order is so by the nature of things, independently of human conventions. All justice comes from God, who is its sole source; but if we knew how to receive so high an inspiration, we would need neither government nor laws. There is, no doubt, a universal justice flowing from reason alone; but for that justice to be admitted among us, it has to be mutual. Humanly speaking, in the absence of natural sanctions, the laws of justice are useless among men: they only serve the wicked and undo the just, when the just man observes them toward everyone and no one observes them toward him. Conventions and laws are therefore needed to join rights to duties and to refer justice to its proper object. In the state of nature, where everything is in common, I owe nothing to a man I have promised nothing; I recognize as belonging to others only what is of no use to me. In the state of society, every right is fixed by law, and the case is different.

But what, then, is a law? As long as we are content to attach purely metaphysical ideas to the word, we will go on arguing without arriving at an understanding; and even when we have defined a law of nature, we will be no closer to the definition of a law of the State.

I have already said that there can be no general will directed at a particular object. Such an object must be either inside or outside the State. If outside, then a will alien to the State cannot be general in relation to it; if inside, it is part of the State, and a relation then arises between whole and part that makes them two separate beings — the part being one, and the whole minus the part being the other. But the whole minus a part is not the whole; and as long as this relation persists, there is no whole, only two unequal parts; from which it follows that the will of the one is no longer in any respect general in relation to the other.

But when the whole people decrees for the whole people, it is considering only itself; and if a relation does form, it is between two aspects of the entire object, with no division of the whole. In that case the matter on which the decree is made is, like the will that decrees it, general. This act is what I call a law.

When I say that the object of laws is always general, I mean that the law considers subjects _en masse_ and actions in the abstract — never a particular person or a particular action. So the law may decree that there shall be privileges, but cannot confer them on any specific person by name. It may set up several classes of citizens, and even lay down the qualifications for membership of those classes, but it cannot name particular persons as belonging to them. It may establish a monarchy and hereditary succession, but it cannot choose a king or designate a royal family. In a word, no function with a particular object belongs to the legislative power.

On this view, we can immediately see that it is no longer a question whose business it is to make laws, since they are acts of the general will; nor whether the prince is above the law, since he is a member of the State; nor whether the law can be unjust, since no one is unjust to himself; nor how we can be both free and subject to the laws, since the laws are nothing but registers of our wills.

We can also see that, since the law unites universality of will with universality of object, what any man, whoever he is, commands on his own initiative cannot be a law; and even what the Sovereign commands with regard to a particular matter is no closer to being a law — it is a decree, an act not of sovereignty but of magistracy.

I therefore give the name “Republic” to every State that is governed by laws, whatever the form of its administration may be: for only in such a case does the public interest govern, and the _res publica_ count as something _real_. Every legitimate government is republican;[1] what government is, I will explain later.

Laws, properly speaking, are simply the conditions of civil association. The people, being subject to the laws, ought to be their author: the conditions of the society ought to be set solely by those who come together to form it. But how are they to set them? By common agreement, by sudden inspiration? Does the body politic have an organ for declaring its will? Who can give it the foresight to formulate and announce its acts in advance? Or how is it to declare them in the moment of need? How can a blind multitude, which often does not know what it wills because it rarely knows what is good for it, carry out, on its own, so great and difficult an enterprise as a system of legislation? Of itself, the people always wills the good, but of itself it does not always see it. The general will is always in the right, but the judgment that guides it is not always enlightened. It must be made to see things as they are, and sometimes as they ought to appear; it must be shown the good road it is searching for, secured against the seductive influences of individual wills, taught to see times and places as a sequence, and made to weigh the attractions of present and tangible advantages against the danger of distant and hidden harms. Individuals see the good they reject; the public wills a good it does not see. Both stand equally in need of guidance. The first must be compelled to bring their wills into line with their reason; the second must be taught to know what it wills. If this is done, public enlightenment leads to the union of understanding and will in the social body: the parts are made to work exactly together, and the whole is raised to its highest power. This is what makes a legislator necessary.

chapters.title: Book 2, Chapter 7 — The Legislator
paragraphs: To discover the rules of society best suited to nations, we would need a superior intelligence that could see all the passions of men without feeling any of them. This intelligence would have to be wholly unrelated to our nature, while knowing it through and through; its happiness would have to be independent of us, and yet it would have to be willing to attend to ours; finally, in the march of time, it would have to look forward to a distant glory, working in one century to enjoy the result in the next.[1] It would take gods to give men laws.

What Caligula argued from the facts, Plato — in the dialogue called the _Politicus_ — argued in defining the civil or kingly man, on the basis of right. But if great princes are rare, how much rarer are great legislators? The first have only to follow the pattern that the second must lay down. The legislator is the engineer who invents the machine; the prince is merely the mechanic who sets it up and makes it run. “At the birth of societies,” says Montesquieu, “the rulers of Republics establish institutions, and afterwards the institutions shape the rulers.”[2]

Anyone who dares to undertake the founding of a people’s institutions must feel himself capable, so to speak, of changing human nature — of transforming each individual, who is by himself a complete and solitary whole, into a part of a greater whole from which he in a sense receives his life and being; of altering the constitution of man in order to strengthen it; of substituting a partial and moral existence for the physical and independent existence nature has given us all. He must, in a word, take from man his own resources and give him in exchange new ones, alien to him, and incapable of being used without the help of other men. The more completely his natural resources are annihilated, the greater and more lasting are the ones he acquires, and the more stable and perfect the new institutions become; so that if each citizen is nothing and can do nothing without the rest, and the resources gained by the whole equal or surpass the sum of the resources of all the individuals, legislation can be said to have reached the highest possible point of perfection.

The legislator occupies, in every respect, an extraordinary position in the State. If he does so by virtue of his genius, he does so no less by virtue of his office, which is neither magistracy nor Sovereignty. This office, which sets up the Republic, has no place in its constitution; it is an individual and superior function, with nothing in common with human empire. For if the man who has command over men ought not to have command over the laws, neither should the man who has command over the laws have it over men — or else his laws would be ministers of his passions, and would often only serve to perpetuate his injustices: his private aims would inevitably mar the sanctity of his work.

When Lycurgus gave laws to his country, he began by resigning the throne. It was the custom of most Greek towns to entrust the establishment of their laws to foreigners. The Republics of modern Italy often followed this example; Geneva did the same and benefited from it.[3] Rome, at the height of its prosperity, suffered a revival of all the crimes of tyranny, and was brought to the brink of destruction, because it placed legislative authority and sovereign power in the same hands.

Yet even the decemvirs themselves never claimed the right to pass any law on their own authority alone. “Nothing we propose to you,” they said to the people, “can pass into law without your consent. Romans, be yourselves the authors of the laws that are to make you happy.”

Whoever drafts the laws, then, has — or should have — no right of legislation, and the people cannot, even if it wishes, deprive itself of this right, which cannot be transferred to another. For according to the fundamental compact, only the general will can bind individuals, and there is no way to be sure a particular will is in conformity with the general will until it has been put to the free vote of the people. I have said this already; but it is worth repeating.
So in the work of legislation we find, side by side, two things that seem incompatible: an enterprise too difficult for human powers, and, for its execution, an authority that is no authority.

There is a further difficulty worth attention. Wise men, if they try to speak their own language to the common crowd instead of the crowd’s, simply cannot make themselves understood. There are a thousand kinds of ideas that are impossible to translate into popular language. Conceptions too general and objects too remote are equally beyond its reach: each individual, having no taste for any plan of government other than the one that suits his particular interest, finds it hard to grasp the advantages he might draw from the steady deprivations that good laws impose. For a young people to relish sound principles of political theory and follow the fundamental rules of statecraft, the effect would have to become the cause; the social spirit, which should be created by these institutions, would have to preside over their very founding; and men would have to be, before law, what they should become through law. Since the legislator can appeal neither to force nor to reason, he must turn to an authority of a different order, capable of compelling without violence and persuading without convincing.

This is what has, in every age, driven the fathers of nations to call on divine intervention and credit the gods with their own wisdom — so that the peoples, submitting to the laws of the State as to those of nature, and recognizing the same power in the formation of the city as in the formation of man, would obey freely and bear with docility the yoke of public happiness.

This sublime reason, far above the reach of the common crowd, is what the legislator puts in the mouth of the immortals, in order to constrain by divine authority those whom human prudence could not move.[4] But not just anyone can make the gods speak, or get himself believed when he proclaims himself their interpreter. The great soul of the legislator is the only miracle that can prove his mission. Any man can engrave tablets of stone, or buy an oracle, or pretend to secret communion with some divinity, or train a bird to whisper in his ear, or find other vulgar tricks to impose on the people. The man whose knowledge goes no further may indeed gather a band of fools around him, but he will never found an empire, and his extravagances will quickly perish with him. Empty tricks form a passing tie; only wisdom can make it lasting. The Judaic law, which still endures, and the law of the child of Ishmael, which has ruled half the world for ten centuries, still proclaim the great men who laid them down; and while the pride of philosophy or the blind spirit of faction sees in them nothing but lucky impostures, the true political theorist admires, in the institutions they set up, the great and powerful genius that presides over things made to endure.

We should not, with Warburton, conclude from this that politics and religion have for us a common object — but rather that, in the first periods of nations, the one is used as an instrument of the other.
