chapters.title: Book 2, Chapter 8 — The People
paragraphs: Just as, before erecting a large building, the architect surveys and tests the site to see if it can bear the weight, the wise legislator does not begin by laying down laws good in themselves, but by examining whether the people for whom they are intended is fit to receive them. Plato refused to legislate for the Arcadians and the Cyrenæans, because he knew both peoples were rich and could not put up with equality; and good laws and bad men were found together in Crete, because Minos had imposed discipline on a people already weighed down by vice.

A thousand nations have achieved earthly greatness that could never have endured good laws; even those that could have endured them could only have done so for a very brief stretch of their long history. Most peoples, like most men, are docile only in youth; as they grow old, they become incorrigible. Once customs have taken root and prejudices have hardened, it is dangerous and useless to attempt their reform; the people, like a foolish and cowardly patient who rages at the sight of the doctor, can no longer bear that anyone should lay hands on its faults to remedy them.

There are indeed times in the history of States when, just as some illnesses turn men’s heads and make them forget the past, periods of violence and revolution do to peoples what these crises do to individuals: horror of the past replaces forgetfulness, and the State, set on fire by civil war, is born again, so to speak, from its ashes, and takes on, fresh from the jaws of death, the vigor of youth. Such were Sparta in the time of Lycurgus, Rome after the Tarquins, and, in modern times, Holland and Switzerland after the expulsion of their tyrants.

But such events are rare; they are exceptions, and their cause is always to be found in the particular constitution of the State concerned. They cannot even happen twice to the same people, for a people can make itself free as long as it is barbarous, but not once the civic impulse has lost its vigor. From that point on, disturbances may destroy it, but revolutions cannot mend it: it needs a master, not a liberator. Free peoples, remember this maxim: “Liberty may be gained, but it can never be recovered.”

Youth is not infancy. For nations, as for men, there is a period of youth — or shall we say, maturity — before which they should not be made subject to laws. But the maturity of a people is not always easy to recognize, and if it is anticipated, the work is spoiled. One people takes to discipline from the start; another, not even after ten centuries. Russia will never be truly civilized, because it was civilized too soon. Peter had a genius for imitation, but he lacked true genius — the kind that is creative and makes everything from nothing. He did some good things, but most of what he did was out of place. He saw that his people was barbarous, but did not see that it was not yet ripe for civilization: he wanted to civilize it when it needed only to be hardened. His first wish was to make Germans or Englishmen, when he ought to have been making Russians; and he kept his subjects from ever becoming what they might have been by persuading them they were what they are not. In the same way, a French teacher turns his pupil into a child prodigy, who for the rest of his life amounts to nothing at all. The empire of Russia will set out to conquer Europe, and will itself be conquered. The Tartars, its subjects or neighbors, will become its masters and ours, by a revolution I regard as inevitable. Indeed, all the kings of Europe are working in concert to hasten its arrival.

chapters.title: Book 2, Chapter 9 — The People (continued)
paragraphs: Just as nature has set limits to the height of a well-made man, and outside those limits produces only giants or dwarfs, so too, for the constitution of a State to be at its best, it is possible to set limits that will make it neither too large for good government, nor too small for self-maintenance. In every body politic there is a _maximum_ strength that it cannot exceed, and that it loses simply by growing larger. Every extension of the social bond means its loosening; and, generally speaking, a small State is proportionally stronger than a great one.

A thousand arguments could be given for this principle. First, long distances make administration more difficult, just as a weight grows heavier at the end of a longer lever. Administration becomes more and more burdensome as distance increases; for, in the first place, each city has its own administration, paid for by the people; each district has its own, still paid for by the people; then comes each province, and then the great governments, satrapies, and viceroyalties, costing more the higher you go, and always at the expense of the unfortunate people. Last comes the supreme administration, which eclipses all the rest. All these added burdens are a continual drain on the subjects; far from being better governed by all these layers of authority, they are worse governed than they would be under a single one. Meanwhile, scarcely enough resources remain to meet emergencies; and when those have to be drawn on, the State is always on the brink of destruction.

That is not all. Not only does the government have less vigor and promptness for ensuring the observance of the laws, preventing nuisances, correcting abuses, and guarding against seditious schemes hatched in distant places — the people also has less affection for its rulers, whom it never sees; for its country, which to its eyes seems like the world; and for its fellow citizens, most of whom are unknown to it. The same laws cannot suit so many diverse provinces, with different customs, situated in the most varied climates, incapable of bearing a uniform government. Different laws lead only to trouble and confusion among peoples who, living under the same rulers and in constant communication with one another, intermingle and intermarry, and, falling under the sway of new customs, never know whether they can call their very inheritance their own. Talent is buried, virtue unknown, and vice unpunished, among such a multitude of men who do not know one another, gathered together in the seat of central administration. The leaders, overwhelmed with business, see nothing for themselves; the State is governed by clerks. Finally, the measures that have to be taken to maintain the general authority — which all these distant officials want to escape or to flout — absorb all the public’s energy, leaving none for the people’s happiness. Hardly enough is left to defend the people in time of need; and so a body too big for its constitution gives way and collapses crushed under its own weight.

Again, the State must give itself a safe foundation, if it is to have stability and to withstand the shocks it cannot help suffering, as well as the efforts it will be forced to make to maintain itself. For all peoples have a kind of centrifugal force that constantly drives them against one another, each tending to grow at its neighbors’ expense, like the vortices of Descartes. The weak therefore risk being swallowed up; and it is almost impossible for any one people to preserve itself except by maintaining an equilibrium with all the others, so that the pressure on every side is roughly equal.

It can be seen, then, that there are reasons for expansion and reasons for contraction; and it is no small part of a statesman’s skill to find between them the mean most favorable to the preservation of the State. The reason for expansion, being merely external and relative, ought to be subordinate to the reasons for contraction, which are internal and absolute. A strong and healthy constitution is the first thing to look for; and it is better to count on the vigor that comes from good government than on the resources a great territory provides.

It may be added that there have been States so constituted that the necessity of making conquests was built into their very constitution, and that, to maintain themselves, they had to expand without ceasing. They may have congratulated themselves greatly on this fortunate necessity — which nonetheless marked out, along with the limits of their greatness, the inevitable moment of their fall.

chapters.title: Book 2, Chapter 10 — The People (continued)
paragraphs: A body politic can be measured in two ways: by the extent of its territory, or by the number of its people. There is, between these two measurements, a right relation that makes a State truly great. The men make the State, and the territory sustains the men; the right relation is therefore that the land should suffice to maintain the inhabitants, and that there should be as many inhabitants as the land can maintain. In this proportion lies the _maximum_ strength of a given number of people; for if there is too much land, it is troublesome to guard, inadequately cultivated, produces more than is needed, and soon gives rise to defensive wars; if there is too little, the State depends on its neighbors for what it lacks, and this soon gives rise to offensive wars. Every people whose situation gives it no choice but between commerce and war is weak in itself: it depends on its neighbors and on circumstances; its existence can only ever be short and uncertain. Either it conquers others and changes its situation, or it is conquered and becomes nothing. Only insignificance or greatness can keep it free.

No fixed ratio can be given between the extent of territory and the population that suit each other, both because of differences in the quality of land — its fertility, the nature of its products, the influence of climate — and because of differences in the temperaments of those who inhabit it. Some people in a fertile country consume little, while others on stingy soil consume much. The greater or lesser fertility of women, the conditions more or less favorable in each country to population growth, and the influence the legislator can hope to exert through his institutions, must also be taken into account. The legislator should therefore go not by what he sees, but by what he foresees; he should pause not so much at the state in which he actually finds the population, as at the state it ought naturally to reach. Finally, there are countless cases in which particular local circumstances demand or allow the acquisition of more territory than seems necessary. Expansion will be great in a mountainous country, where the natural products — woods and pastures — require less labor, where experience teaches that women are more fertile than on the plains, and where a great expanse of slope yields only a small level area on which vegetation can be relied on. On the other hand, contraction is possible on the coast, even in lands of rocks and nearly barren sands, because there fishing makes up for much of the lack of land produce, the inhabitants have to gather more closely together to repel pirates, and it is also easier to relieve the country of its surplus inhabitants by way of colonies.

To these conditions for lawgiving must be added one more which, though it cannot replace the others, makes them all useless when it is missing: the enjoyment of peace and plenty. The moment when a State sets its house in order is, like the moment when a battalion is forming up, the moment when its body is least able to offer resistance and easiest to destroy. Better resistance could be made in a state of total disorganization than at a moment of fermentation, when each is occupied with his own position and not with the danger. If war, famine, or sedition arises at this moment of crisis, the State will inevitably be overthrown.

Not that many governments have not been set up in such storms; but in those cases, these governments are themselves the destroyers of the State. Usurpers always bring about, or single out, troubled times to push through, under cover of public terror, destructive laws that the people would never adopt in cold blood. The choice of the moment is one of the surest ways to tell the work of the legislator from that of the tyrant.

What people, then, is fit to be legislated for? One that, already bound together by some unity of origin, interest, or convention, has not yet felt the real yoke of law; one whose customs and superstitions are not deeply ingrained; one in no fear of being overwhelmed by sudden invasion; one that, without entering into its neighbors’ quarrels, can resist any of them on its own, or get the help of one to repel another; one in which every member can be known by every other, and where there is no need to lay on any man burdens too heavy for a man to bear; one that can do without other peoples, and without which all others can do;[1] one neither rich nor poor, but self-sufficient; and finally, one that combines the consistency of an ancient people with the docility of a new one. Legislation is made difficult less by what has to be built up than by what has to be torn down; and what makes success so rare is the impossibility of finding natural simplicity together with social requirements. All these conditions are indeed rarely found together, and that is why few States have good constitutions.

There is still in Europe one country capable of receiving laws — Corsica. The valor and persistence with which that brave people has regained and defended its liberty well deserves that some wise man should teach it how to preserve what it has won. I have a feeling that someday that little island will astonish Europe.

The Republic of Thlascala, surrounded by the Mexican Empire, preferred doing without salt to buying it from the Mexicans, or even accepting it as a gift. The Thlascalans were wise enough to see the trap hidden under such generosity. chapters.title: Book 2, Chapter 11 — The Various Systems of Legislation
paragraphs: If we ask in what, precisely, the greatest good of all consists — which should be the end of every system of legislation — we will find it reduces to two main objects: liberty and equality. Liberty, because every particular dependence means just that much force taken from the body of the State; and equality, because liberty cannot exist without it.

I have already defined civil liberty. By equality, we should not understand that the degrees of power and wealth are to be absolutely identical for everyone, but rather that power should never be great enough for violence, and should always be exercised by virtue of rank and law; and that, with regard to wealth, no citizen should ever be rich enough to buy another, and none poor enough to be forced to sell himself.[1] This implies, on the side of the great, moderation in goods and position, and on the side of the common sort, moderation in greed and covetousness.

Such equality, we are told, is an unworkable ideal that cannot exist in practice. But if its abuse is inevitable, does it follow that we should not at least make rules about it? It is precisely because the force of circumstances continually tends to destroy equality that the force of legislation should always tend to maintain it.

But these general aims of every good legislative system need to be modified in each country according to the local situation and the temperament of the inhabitants; and these circumstances should determine, in each case, the particular system of institutions that is best — not perhaps in itself, but for the State for which it is intended. If, for instance, the soil is barren and unproductive, or the land too crowded for its inhabitants, the people should turn to industry and the crafts, and exchange what they produce for the goods they lack. If, on the other hand, a people lives on rich plains and fertile slopes, or, in a good land, lacks inhabitants, it should give all its attention to agriculture, which causes men to multiply, and should drive out the crafts, which would only result in depopulation by clustering the few inhabitants there are in a few localities.[2] If a nation lives on an extensive and convenient coastline, let it cover the sea with ships and foster commerce and navigation. It will have a life that is short and glorious. If, on its coasts, the sea washes nothing but nearly inaccessible rocks, let it remain barbarous and ichthyophagous: it will have a quieter, perhaps a better, and certainly a happier life. In a word, beyond the principles common to all, every nation has within itself something that gives those principles a particular application, and makes its legislation peculiarly its own. So among the Jews long ago, and more recently among the Arabs, the chief object was religion; among the Athenians, letters; at Carthage and Tyre, commerce; at Rhodes, shipping; at Sparta, war; at Rome, virtue. The author of _The Spirit of the Laws_ has shown with many examples by what art the legislator directs the constitution toward each of these objects.

What makes the constitution of a State really solid and lasting is the proper observance of what is fitting, so that the natural relations always agree with the laws on every point, and the law only serves, so to speak, to secure, accompany, and correct them. But if the legislator mistakes his object and adopts a principle other than what circumstances naturally direct — if his principle tends toward servitude while they tend toward liberty, or toward riches while they tend toward populousness, or toward peace while they tend toward conquest — the laws will gradually lose their influence, the constitution will alter, and the State will know no rest from trouble until it is either destroyed or transformed, and nature has resumed her invincible sway.

chapters.title: Book 2, Chapter 12 — The Division of the Laws
paragraphs: If the whole is to be set in order, and the commonwealth shaped as well as possible, several relations must be considered. First, there is the action of the complete body upon itself: the relation of the whole to the whole, of the Sovereign to the State; and this relation, as we shall see, is made up of the relations of the intermediate terms.

The laws regulating this relation bear the name of political laws, and are also called fundamental laws — not without reason, if they are wise. For if there is in each State only one good system, the people that has it should hold fast to it; but if the established order is bad, why should laws that prevent men from being good be regarded as fundamental? Besides, in any case, a people is always in a position to change its laws, however good they are; for if it chooses to do itself harm, who has the right to stop it?

The second relation is that of the members to one another, or to the body as a whole; and this relation should be, in the first respect, as small as possible, and in the second, as large as possible. Each citizen would then be perfectly independent of every other, and at the same time fully dependent on the city — a result always achieved by the same means, since only the strength of the State can secure the liberty of its members. From this second relation arise civil laws.

We can also consider a third kind of relation between the individual and the law — a relation of disobedience to its penalty. This gives rise to criminal laws, which, at bottom, are less a particular class of laws than the sanction behind all the rest.

Along with these three kinds of law goes a fourth, the most important of all, which is engraved not on tablets of marble or brass but on the hearts of the citizens. This forms the real constitution of the State; takes on new powers each day; restores the others or takes their place when they decay or die out; keeps a people on the path it was meant to follow; and silently replaces authority with the force of habit. I am speaking of morality, of custom, above all of public opinion — a power unknown to political thinkers, on which nevertheless the success of everything else depends. With this the great legislator concerns himself in secret, even while he seems to confine himself to particular regulations; for these are only the arc of the arch, while manners and morals, slower to take shape, in the end form its immovable keystone.
Among the different classes of laws, only the political laws — those that determine the form of government — are relevant to my subject.

chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 1 — Government in General
paragraphs: Before talking about the different forms of government, let us try to fix the precise sense of the word, which has not yet been clearly explained.
I warn the reader that this chapter requires careful reading, and that I cannot make myself clear to those who refuse to be attentive.

Every free action is produced by the meeting of two causes: one moral — the will, which decides the act; the other physical — the power that executes it. When I walk toward an object, I must first will to go there, and second, my feet must carry me. If a paralytic wills to run and an active man wills not to, both will stay where they are. The body politic has the same motive forces; here too force and will are distinguished — will under the name of legislative power, and force under the name of executive power. Without their concurrence, nothing is, or should be, done.

We have seen that legislative power belongs to the people, and can belong only to it. From the principles laid down above, it can readily be seen that executive power cannot belong to the generality acting as legislature or Sovereign, because it consists wholly of particular acts that fall outside the competence of the law, and so outside the competence of the Sovereign, whose acts must always be laws.

The public force therefore needs an agent of its own to bind it together and set it to work under the direction of the general will, to serve as a means of communication between the State and the Sovereign, and to do for the collective person more or less what the union of soul and body does for a man. This is what, within the State, is the basis of government — often wrongly confused with the Sovereign, of which it is merely the minister.

What, then, is government? An intermediate body set up between the subjects and the Sovereign to ensure their mutual correspondence, charged with the execution of the laws and the maintenance of liberty, both civil and political.

The members of this body are called magistrates or _kings_ — that is, _governors_ — and the body as a whole bears the name _prince_.[1] Those who hold that the act by which a people places itself under a prince is not a contract are therefore right. It is simply and solely a commission, an employment, in which the rulers, as mere officials of the Sovereign, exercise in their own name the power of which it makes them trustees. This power can be limited, modified, or revoked at the Sovereign’s pleasure; for the alienation of such a right is incompatible with the nature of the social body, and contrary to the end of association.
I therefore call _government_, or supreme administration, the legitimate exercise of the executive power, and prince or magistrate the man or body entrusted with that administration.

In government reside the intermediate forces whose relations make up the relation of the whole to the whole, or of the Sovereign to the State. This last relation can be represented as that between the extreme terms of a continuous proportion, in which the government is the mean proportional. The government receives from the Sovereign the orders it gives the people, and, for the State to be properly balanced, all things considered, there must be equality between the product or power of the government taken in itself, and the product or power of the citizens, who are on one side sovereign and on the other subjects.

Moreover, none of these three terms can be altered without the equality being instantly destroyed. If the Sovereign tries to govern, or the magistrate to make laws, or the subjects refuse to obey, disorder replaces regularity, force and will no longer act together, and the State dissolves into despotism or anarchy. Finally, since there is only one mean proportional between any given relation, there is also only one good government possible for any given State. But since countless events can change the relations of a people, not only may different governments be good for different peoples, but also for the same people at different times.
To give some idea of the various relations that may hold between these two extreme terms, I will take as an example the size of a population, which is the most easily expressed.

Suppose the State is composed of ten thousand citizens. The Sovereign can be considered only collectively and as a body; but each member, being a subject, is regarded as an individual. So the Sovereign stands to the subject as ten thousand to one — that is, each member of the State has only a ten-thousandth share of the sovereign authority, although he is wholly under its control. If the people numbers a hundred thousand, the condition of the subject does not change, and each is equally under the whole authority of the laws, while his vote, reduced to a hundred-thousandth part, has ten times less influence in drawing them up. The subject therefore remains a unit, and the relation between him and the Sovereign grows with the number of citizens. From this it follows that the larger the State, the less the liberty.

When I say the relation increases, I mean that it grows more unequal. So the greater it is in the geometric sense, the less relation there is in the ordinary sense of the word. In the first sense, the relation considered by quantity is expressed by a quotient; in the second, considered by identity, it is reckoned by similarity.

Now, the less relation there is between particular wills and the general will — that is, between morals and manners on one side and laws on the other — the more the repressive force should be increased. To be good, then, the government should be proportionally stronger as the people grows more numerous.

On the other hand, since the growth of the State gives the trustees of public authority more temptations and opportunities to abuse their power, the greater the force the government must be given to keep the people in hand, the greater too must be the force the Sovereign has at its disposal to keep the government in hand. I am speaking not of absolute force, but of the relative force of the State’s different parts.

It follows from this double relation that the continuous proportion between Sovereign, prince, and people is by no means an arbitrary idea, but a necessary consequence of the nature of the body politic. It also follows that, since one of the extreme terms — the people, as subject — is fixed and represented by unity, whenever the duplicate ratio rises or falls, the simple ratio does the same and is changed accordingly. From this we see that there is no single absolute form of government, but as many governments differing in nature as there are States differing in size.

If, in mocking this system, someone were to say that, in order to find the mean proportional and form the body of the government, all I need to do is take the square root of the population, I would answer that I am taking that number only as an example; that the relations I am describing are not measured by the number of men alone, but more generally by the amount of action, which is a combination of many causes; and that, further, if for the sake of brevity I borrow geometric terms for a moment, I am still well aware that moral quantities do not allow of geometric precision.

The government is on a small scale what the body politic that contains it is on a large one. It is a moral person endowed with certain faculties — active like the Sovereign and passive like the State — and capable of being broken down into other similar relations. This gives rise to a new proportion, within which is yet another, depending on the arrangement of the magistracies, until an indivisible middle term is reached: a single ruler or supreme magistrate, who can be represented, in the middle of this progression, as the unit between the fractional and the ordinal series.

Without burdening ourselves with this multiplication of terms, let us be content to view the government as a new body within the State, distinct from the people and the Sovereign, and intermediate between them.

There is between these two bodies an essential difference: the State exists by itself, while the government exists only through the Sovereign. The dominant will of the prince is, or should be, nothing other than the general will, or the law; his force is only the public force concentrated in his hands. As soon as he tries to base any absolute and independent act on his own authority, the bond holding the whole together begins to loosen. If finally the prince comes to have a particular will more active than the will of the Sovereign, and uses the public force in his hands in obedience to that particular will, there will be, so to speak, two Sovereigns — one rightful, the other actual; the social union will instantly evaporate, and the body politic dissolve.

However, in order for the government to have a true existence and a real life distinguishing it from the body of the State, and in order for all its members to act in concert and fulfill the end for which it was set up, it must have a particular personality, a sensibility shared by its members, and a force and will of its own directed at its preservation. This particular existence implies assemblies, councils, the power of deliberation and decision, rights, titles, and privileges belonging exclusively to the prince — and making the office of magistrate more honorable in proportion as it is more burdensome. The difficulty lies in arranging this subordinate whole within the whole in such a way that it does not alter the general constitution by asserting its own; that it always distinguishes the particular force it possesses, intended for its own preservation, from the public force, which is intended for the preservation of the State; and, in a word, is always ready to sacrifice the government to the people, never the people to the government.

Furthermore, although the artificial body of the government is the work of another artificial body, and has, we may say, only a borrowed and subordinate life, this does not stop it from acting with more or less vigor or promptness, or from being, so to speak, in more or less robust health. Finally, without departing entirely from the end for which it was instituted, it can deviate more or less from it, depending on the manner of its constitution.

From all these differences arise the various relations the government ought to bear to the body of the State, according to the accidental and particular relations by which the State itself is modified; for often the government best in itself will become the most pernicious, if the relations in which it stands have altered according to the defects of the body politic to which it belongs.

chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 2 — The Constituent Principle in the Various Forms of Government
paragraphs: To set out the general cause of the differences just mentioned, we must here distinguish between government and its principle, just as we earlier distinguished between the State and the Sovereign.

The body of the magistrate may be made up of a greater or lesser number of members. We said that the relation of the Sovereign to the subjects grows in proportion as the people becomes more numerous; by a clear analogy, the same can be said of the relation of the government to the magistrates.
But the total force of the government, being always that of the State, is invariable; so the more of this force it spends on its own members, the less it has left to use on the people as a whole.
The more numerous the magistrates, then, the weaker the government. Since this principle is fundamental, we must do our best to make it clear.

In the person of the magistrate we can distinguish three essentially different wills: first, the private will of the individual, aiming only at his personal advantage; second, the common will of the magistrates, which relates solely to the advantage of the prince and may be called the corporate will, being general in relation to the government and particular in relation to the State, of which the government forms a part; and third, the will of the people, or the sovereign will, which is general both in relation to the State considered as the whole and in relation to the government considered as a part of the whole.

In a perfect act of legislation, the individual or particular will should be at zero; the corporate will belonging to the government should hold a very subordinate place; and consequently the general or sovereign will should always predominate, and be the sole guide of all the rest.

By the natural order, however, these different wills become more active in proportion as they are more concentrated. So the general will is always the weakest, the corporate will second, and the individual will the strongest of all: in the government, then, each member is first himself, then a magistrate, and only then a citizen — exactly the reverse of what the social system requires.

This granted: if the whole government is in the hands of one man, the particular and the corporate will are entirely united, and the corporate will is therefore at the highest possible degree of intensity. But since the use to which force is put depends on the degree of the will, and the absolute force of the government is invariable, it follows that the most active government is the government of one man.

Suppose, on the other hand, that we unite the government with the legislative authority, making the Sovereign also the prince and all the citizens so many magistrates. Then the corporate will, being merged with the general will, can have no more activity than that will, and must leave the particular will as strong as it can possibly be. The government, retaining always the same absolute force, will then be at its lowest point of relative force or activity.

These relations are beyond dispute, and there are other considerations that further confirm them. We can see, for instance, that each magistrate is more active in the body to which he belongs than each citizen is in his, and that consequently the particular will has much more influence on the acts of the government than on those of the Sovereign. Each magistrate is almost always charged with some governmental function, while each citizen, taken alone, exercises no function of Sovereignty. Moreover, the bigger the State grows, the more its real force increases, though not in direct proportion to its growth; but, the State remaining the same, the number of magistrates may rise indefinitely without the government gaining any more real force, since its force is that of the State, whose dimensions remain the same. Thus the relative force or activity of the government decreases, while its absolute or real force cannot increase.

It is also certain that promptness in execution diminishes as more people are put in charge of it: where prudence is overdone, fortune is undervalued; the opportunity is let slip, and deliberation results in losing what was at stake.

I have just shown that the government grows slack as the number of magistrates increases; and I showed earlier that the more numerous the people, the greater the repressive force should be. From this it follows that the relation of the magistrates to the government should vary inversely to the relation of the subjects to the Sovereign — that is, the larger the State, the more the government should be tightened, so that the number of rulers diminishes in proportion as the number of the people increases.

It should be added that I am speaking here of the relative strength of the government, not its rectitude. For, on the other hand, the more numerous the magistracy, the closer the corporate will comes to the general will, while under a single magistrate the corporate will is, as I said, merely a particular will. So what may be gained on one side is lost on the other, and the legislator’s art is to know how to fix the point at which the force and the will of the government — which are always in inverse proportion — meet in the relation most advantageous to the State.

chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 3 — The Division of Governments
paragraphs: We saw in the last chapter what causes the various kinds or forms of government to be distinguished by the number of members composing them; it remains in this one to discover how the division is made.

First, the Sovereign may commit the charge of government to the whole people, or to the majority of the people, so that more citizens are magistrates than are mere private individuals. This form of government is called _democracy_.
Or it may restrict the government to a smaller number, so that there are more private citizens than magistrates; this is called _aristocracy_.

Finally, it may concentrate the whole government in the hands of a single magistrate, from whom all others derive their power. This third form is the most usual, and is called _monarchy_, or royal government.

It should be noted that all these forms — at least the first two — admit of degrees, and even of very wide differences. Democracy may include the whole people, or be restricted to half. Aristocracy, in turn, may be narrowed indefinitely from half the people down to the smallest possible number. Even royalty admits of some distribution. Sparta always had two kings, as its constitution provided; and the Roman Empire saw as many as eight emperors at once, without it being possible to say that the Empire was split apart. There is, then, a point at which each form of government passes into the next; and it becomes clear that, under three broad headings, government is really capable of as many different forms as the State has citizens.

There are even more: for since the government can also, in certain respects, be subdivided into other parts — one administered one way, another differently — the combination of the three forms can produce a multitude of mixed forms, each of which can in turn be multiplied by all the simple forms.
There has, in every age, been much dispute about the best form of government, without taking into account that each is in some cases the best and in others the worst.

If, in different States, the number of supreme magistrates should stand in inverse ratio to the number of citizens, it follows that, generally, democratic government suits small States, aristocratic government those of middle size, and monarchy great ones. This rule follows directly from the principle laid down. But it is impossible to count all the innumerable circumstances that may produce exceptions.

chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 4 — Democracy
paragraphs: Whoever makes a law understands better than anyone else how it ought to be applied and interpreted. It would therefore seem that no constitution could improve on one that joins legislative and executive power. Yet that very union makes the government inadequate in certain ways: it confuses things that ought to remain distinct. When the prince and the Sovereign are the same person, the result is, so to speak, a government with no government of its own.

It is unwise for the maker of laws to carry them out, or for the people as a body to abandon their general outlook and give their attention to particular matters. Nothing threatens public affairs more than the intrusion of private interests. A government's abuse of the laws is a smaller evil than the corruption of the legislator, which inevitably follows when he takes a particular view. Once that happens, the State has changed in its very substance, and reform is no longer possible. A people that never abused the powers of government would never abuse its independence either; a people that always governed well would have no need to be governed.

Taken in its strict meaning, real democracy has never existed and never will. The natural order does not allow the many to rule while the few are ruled. We cannot imagine the people staying permanently assembled so that they can spend their time on public business. And plainly, if they appoint commissions to do that work, they have already changed the form of their administration.

Indeed, I can confidently state this principle: when several tribunals share the work of government, those with fewer members eventually gain the most authority. Even if there were no other reason, their ability to deal with business more quickly would naturally bring power into their hands.

Besides, how many requirements such a government assumes, and how difficult they are to bring together! First, the State must be very small, so that its people can assemble readily and every citizen can easily know all the others. Second, their way of life must be very simple, so that business does not multiply and produce difficult problems. Next, there must be considerable equality of rank and wealth, since equal rights and authority cannot last long without it. Finally, there must be little luxury, or none at all--luxury either arises from wealth or creates a need for it. It corrupts rich and poor alike: the rich through ownership, the poor through envy. It sells the country to comfort and vanity, depriving the State of all its citizens by making them slaves to one another, and all of them slaves to public opinion.

That is why a famous writer made virtue the basic principle of Republics: none of these conditions could exist without it. But that great thinker failed to draw the necessary distinctions, and so was often imprecise and sometimes unclear. He did not recognise that sovereign authority is the same everywhere. The same principle must therefore exist in every properly constituted State, though admittedly in a greater or smaller degree according to the form its government takes.

We may add that no government is more exposed to civil war and internal unrest than democratic or popular government. None has so powerful and persistent a tendency to turn into another form, and none requires greater vigilance and courage to preserve it as it is. Under this constitution above all others, the citizen must equip himself with firmness and perseverance. Every day of his life he should repeat what a virtuous Count Palatine[1] said in the Diet of Poland: Malo periculosam libertatem quam quietum servitium.
If a people made up of gods existed, it would govern itself democratically. A government so perfect is beyond human beings.

chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 5 — Aristocracy
paragraphs: Here we have two quite distinct moral persons — the government and the Sovereign — and consequently two general wills: one general in relation to all the citizens, the other only in relation to the members of the administration. So although the government may regulate its internal policy as it pleases, it can never speak to the people except in the name of the Sovereign — that is, of the people itself. This must not be forgotten.

The first societies governed themselves aristocratically. The heads of families took counsel together on public affairs. The young bowed without question to the authority of experience. Hence such names as _priests, elders, senate_, and _gerontes_. The savages of North America still govern themselves this way today, and their government is admirable.

But as the artificial inequality produced by institutions came to outweigh natural inequality, riches or power[1] were placed before age, and aristocracy became elective. Finally, the transmission of the father’s power, along with his goods, to his children — by creating patrician families — made government hereditary, and there came to be senators of twenty.

There are, then, three kinds of aristocracy: natural, elective, and hereditary. The first suits only simple peoples; the third is the worst of all governments; the second is the best, and is aristocracy properly so called.

Beyond the advantage of distinguishing the two powers, this form has the advantage of having its members chosen; for under popular government all citizens are born magistrates, but here magistracy is restricted to a few, who become such only by election.[2] By this means, integrity, understanding, experience, and every other claim to pre-eminence and public esteem become so many further guarantees of wise government.

Moreover, assemblies are more easily held, business is better discussed and conducted with more order and diligence, and the State’s credit abroad is better sustained by venerable senators than by a multitude that is unknown or despised.

In a word, it is the best and most natural arrangement that the wisest should govern the many — provided one is sure they will govern for the people’s benefit and not for their own. There is no need to multiply instruments, or to use twenty thousand men to do what a hundred picked men can do better. But it must not be forgotten that here corporate interest begins to direct the public power less under the regulation of the general will, and that a further inevitable tendency takes part of the executive power away from the laws.

As to what is desirable in itself: the State should be neither so small, nor a people so simple and upright, that the execution of the laws follows immediately from the public will, as in a good democracy; nor should the nation be so great that the rulers, in order to govern it, have to scatter and play the Sovereign each in his own department — and, beginning by making themselves independent, end by becoming masters.

But if aristocracy does not require all the virtues needed by popular government, it requires others peculiar to itself: moderation on the side of the rich, and contentment on the side of the poor. For thoroughgoing equality would seem out of place — it was not even found at Sparta.

Furthermore, if this form of government carries with it a certain inequality of fortune, this is justifiable so that, as a rule, the administration of public affairs may be entrusted to those most able to give it their whole time — but not, as Aristotle holds, so that the rich should always be put first. On the contrary, it is important that the opposite choice be made occasionally, to teach the people that men’s deserts give claims to pre-eminence more important than wealth does.

The first has therefore long been a State dissolved; the second, however, is maintained by the extreme wisdom of its senate, and forms an honorable and highly dangerous exception.

chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 6 — Monarchy
paragraphs: So far, we have considered the prince as a moral and collective person, unified by the force of the laws and serving in the State as the trustee of the executive power. We must now consider this power when it is gathered into the hands of a natural person, a real man, who alone has the right to dispose of it in accordance with the laws. Such a person is called a monarch, or king.

In contrast with other forms of administration, in which a collective being represents an individual, in this form an individual represents a collective being; so that the moral unity that constitutes the prince is at the same time a physical unity, and all the qualities that the law brings together only with difficulty in other forms are here naturally united.

Thus the will of the people, the will of the prince, the public force of the State, and the particular force of the government all answer to a single motive power; all the springs of the machine are in the same hands; the whole moves toward the same end; there are no conflicting movements canceling each other; and no kind of constitution can be imagined in which a smaller amount of effort produces a greater amount of action. Archimedes, sitting calmly on the bank and easily drawing a great vessel afloat, is to my mind the image of a skilful monarch, governing vast states from his study, and moving everything while he seems himself unmoved.

But if no government is more vigorous than this one, none is more dominated by the particular will, or in which the particular will more easily rules the rest. Everything moves toward the same end, indeed — but that end is by no means the public happiness, and even the force of the administration constantly proves harmful to the State.

Kings want to be absolute, and from afar men are always crying out to them that the best way to be so is to make their people love them. The advice is fine, and even, in some respects, very true. Unfortunately, it will always be laughed at in court. The power that comes from a people’s love is no doubt the greatest, but it is precarious and conditional, and princes will never be content with it. The best kings want to be in a position to be wicked, if they please, without losing their mastery: political preachers may tell them all they like that, the people’s strength being their own, their first interest is that the people should be prosperous, numerous, and formidable. They know perfectly well this is not so. Their first personal interest is that the people should be weak, wretched, and unable to resist them. I admit that, provided the subjects always remained in submission, the prince’s interest would indeed be that they be powerful, so that their power, being his own, might make him formidable to his neighbors. But since this interest is merely secondary and subordinate, and since strength is incompatible with submission, princes naturally always prefer the principle most immediately to their advantage. This is what Samuel made forcefully plain to the Hebrews, and what Machiavelli clearly demonstrated. He claimed to be teaching kings, but it was the people he was really teaching. His _Prince_ is the book of Republicans.[1]

We found, on general grounds, that monarchy is suitable only for great States, and this is confirmed when we examine it on its own. The more numerous the public administration, the smaller the relation between the prince and his subjects, and the closer it comes to equality, so that in democracy the ratio is unity, or absolute equality. As the government is restricted in number, the ratio increases and reaches its _maximum_ when the government is in the hands of a single person. There is then too great a distance between prince and people, and the State lacks a bond of union. To form such a bond, there must be intermediate orders, with princes, dignitaries, and nobility to make them up. But none of this suits a small State, where all class differences mean ruin.
If, however, it is hard for a great State to be well governed, it is much harder for it to be so by a single man; and everyone knows what happens when kings appoint others to rule for them.

An essential and inevitable defect, which will always rank monarchical below republican government, is that in a republic the public voice almost never raises to the highest positions men who are not enlightened and capable, and worthy of filling them with honor; whereas in monarchies, those who rise to the top are most often petty bunglers, petty swindlers, and petty schemers, whose petty talents help them rise to the highest positions at Court, but, once there, only serve to make their incompetence plain to the public. The people is far less often mistaken in its choice than the prince; and a man of real worth among a king’s ministers is almost as rare as a fool at the head of a republican government. So when, by some lucky chance, one of these born governors takes the helm of a State in some monarchy nearly overwhelmed by swarms of “gentlemanly” administrators, there is nothing but amazement at the resources he uncovers, and his arrival marks an era in his country’s history.

For a monarchical State to have any chance of being well governed, its population and extent must be proportionate to the abilities of its governor. It is easier to conquer than to rule. With a long enough lever, the world could be moved by a single finger; but to hold it up requires the shoulders of Hercules. However small a State may be, the prince is hardly ever big enough for it. When, on the other hand, the State is too small for its ruler, in those rare cases too it is badly governed, because the ruler, constantly pursuing his great designs, forgets the interests of the people, and makes them no less wretched by misusing the talents he has than a less able ruler would by lacking them. A kingdom should, so to speak, expand or contract with each reign, depending on the prince’s capabilities; but since the abilities of a senate are more constant in quantity, the State can have permanent borders without the administration suffering.

The disadvantage most felt in monarchical government is the lack of the continuous succession that, in both other forms, provides an unbroken bond of union. When one king dies, another is needed; elections leave dangerous intervals and are full of storms; and unless the citizens are disinterested and upright to a degree rarely found under this kind of government, intrigue and corruption flourish. The man to whom the State has sold itself can hardly help selling it in turn, recovering at the expense of the weak the money the powerful have squeezed out of him. Under such an administration, venality sooner or later spreads through every part, and the peace enjoyed under a king is worse than the disorders of an interregnum.

What has been done to prevent these evils? Crowns have been made hereditary in certain families, and an order of succession has been set up to keep disputes from arising on the death of kings. That is, the disadvantages of regency have been substituted for those of election; apparent tranquility has been preferred to wise administration, and men have chosen to risk having children, monsters, or imbeciles as rulers rather than dispute the choice of good kings. They did not consider that, in exposing themselves to the risks this entails, they are putting almost all the chances against themselves. There was sound sense in what the younger Dionysius said to his father, who reproached him for some shameful deed by asking, “Did I set you the example?” “No,” said his son, “but your father was not king.”

Everything conspires to deprive a man set in authority over others of his sense of justice and reason. Much trouble, we are told, is taken to teach young princes the art of reigning; but their education seems to do them no good. It would be better to begin by teaching them the art of obeying. The greatest kings whose praises history sings were not brought up to reign: reigning is a science we are never further from possessing than when we have learned too much of it, and one we acquire better by obeying than by commanding. “Nam utilissimus idem ac brevissimus bonarum malarumque rerum delectus cogitare quid aut nolueris sub alio principe, aut volueris.”[2]

One result of this lack of coherence is the inconstancy of royal government, which, regulated now on one scheme and now on another, depending on the character of the reigning prince or those who reign for him, cannot for long have a fixed object or a consistent policy. This variability — not found in the other forms of government, where the prince is always the same — keeps the State always shifting from principle to principle and from project to project. So we may say that, generally, if a court is more cunning in intrigue, there is more wisdom in a senate, and Republics advance toward their ends with more consistent and better-considered policies; whereas every revolution in a royal ministry produces a revolution in the State, since the principle common to all ministers and almost all kings is to do, in every respect, the opposite of what their predecessors did.

This incoherence also clears up a sophism very familiar to royalist political writers. Not only is civil government compared to domestic government and the prince to the father of a family — that error has already been refuted — but the prince is also freely credited with all the virtues he ought to have, and is supposed always to be what he should be. Once that supposition is granted, royal government is clearly preferable to all others, since it is unquestionably the strongest, and only lacks, to be also the best, a corporate will more in line with the general will.

But if, according to Plato,[3] the “king by nature” is such a rarity, how often will nature and fortune conspire to give him a crown? And if royal education necessarily corrupts those who receive it, what can be hoped from a series of men brought up to reign? It is, then, willful self-deception to confuse royal government with government by a good king. To see royal government as it really is, we must consider it under princes who are incompetent or wicked: for either they will come to the throne wicked or incompetent, or the throne will make them so.

These difficulties have not escaped our writers, who all the same are not troubled by them. The remedy, they say, is to obey without a murmur: God sends bad kings in His wrath, and they must be borne as the scourges of Heaven. Such talk is no doubt edifying; but it would be more in place in a pulpit than in a political book. What are we to think of a doctor who promises miracles, and whose whole art is to urge the sufferer to be patient? We know for ourselves that we must put up with a bad government when there is one; the question is how to find a good one.

chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 7 — Mixed Governments
paragraphs: Strictly understood, no government is entirely simple. A ruler acting alone still needs subordinate magistrates, while a government of the people needs a head. Executive power is therefore always distributed in a hierarchy that runs from the larger number to the smaller. The difference is that in some cases the larger number depends on the smaller, while in others the smaller depends on the larger.

Sometimes power is distributed equally. Either the parts depend on one another, as they do in England's government, or each part has authority that is independent but incomplete, as in Poland. This second arrangement is defective: it gives the government no unity, and leaves the State with nothing to bind it together.

Which is better, simple government or mixed government? Political writers continually argue about this. We must answer it as we have already answered the question concerning forms of government in general.

Considered in itself, simple government is better precisely because of its simplicity. But executive power may not depend sufficiently on legislative power--_i.e._ the prince may stand closer to the Sovereign than the people stand to the prince. This disproportion must then be corrected by dividing the government. Each of its parts retains just as much authority over the subjects, but the division reduces their combined strength against the Sovereign.

Appointing intermediate magistrates can prevent the same difficulty. They keep the government intact, serving only to balance the two powers and preserve the rights belonging to each. In that case the government is moderated rather than mixed.

The reverse difficulties can be treated in a similar way. If government is too loose, tribunals can be established to concentrate its power; every democracy does this. In the first case government is divided so as to weaken it, in the second so as to strengthen it. Simple governments reach the _maxima_ of both strength and weakness; mixed forms produce an intermediate degree of strength.

chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 8 — That All Forms of Government Do Not Suit All Countries
paragraphs: Liberty does not grow in every climate, and so it is not available to every people. The longer we examine this principle of Montesquieu's, the more clearly we feel its truth. The more people dispute it, the more opportunities they provide for fresh evidence to confirm it.

Under every government, the public person consumes but produces nothing. Where, then, does its consumption come from? From the labour of its members. The public's needs are met from what individuals have left over. The civil State can therefore survive only while men's labour produces more than they themselves need to live.

The size of this surplus varies from country to country. Some have a large one, some a moderate one, others none, and some even a deficit. The relation between production and subsistence depends on how fertile the climate is, what labour the land requires, what it produces, how strong the inhabitants are, and how much or how little they need to consume. These and several further considerations together determine the whole relationship.

On the other hand, governments themselves differ in nature: some have smaller appetites than others. Their differences rest on this second principle: the farther public contributions travel from their source, the heavier the burden they impose.

To measure that burden, consider not how much is levied but how far the payments must travel before returning to the people who supplied them. If circulation is quick and securely established, it makes no difference whether the payments are large or small: the people remain rich and their financial condition is sound. Conversely, however little the people pay, if that little never returns, continual payment soon drains them. In that case the State is never wealthy, and the people remain a nation of beggars.

Consequently, as the distance between government and people grows, taxation becomes a heavier burden. In a democracy the people therefore carry the lightest load; in an aristocracy, a heavier one; under monarchy, the heaviest of all. Monarchy is thus suited only to wealthy nations, aristocracy to States of moderate size and wealth, and democracy to small, poor States.

Indeed, reflection increasingly reveals this difference between free States and monarchies. In free States everything serves the public good. In monarchies public power and private power act against one another, each growing as the other weakens. Finally, despotism does not govern its subjects in order to make them happy: it makes them miserable in order to govern them.
Every climate, then, has natural causes that allow us to determine the form of government it requires. We can even say what kind of inhabitants ought to live there.

Harsh, barren lands, whose produce does not repay the labour spent on them, should stay deserted and uncultivated, or be inhabited only by savages. Where labour yields no more than the exact _minimum_ needed to live, barbarous peoples should dwell: no political organisation is possible there. Land whose produce leaves only a moderate surplus over labour suits free peoples. Where the soil is rich and fertile, giving a great yield for little work, monarchical government is called for. The prince's luxury can then consume the subjects' excess abundance, since government does better to absorb this surplus than individuals do to squander it among themselves. I know that exceptions exist. Yet the exceptions themselves confirm the rule: sooner or later they bring about revolutions that return things to their natural order.

We must always separate general laws from particular causes that can alter their effects. Suppose Republics covered the entire South and despotic States the entire North. It would still be true, as far as climate is concerned, that despotism suits hot countries, barbarism cold ones, and sound political organisation temperate regions. I also recognise that people may accept the principle and still dispute its application. They may point to very fertile cold countries and very unproductive tropical ones. This objection troubles only those who fail to look at every aspect of the question. As I have already said, we must include labour, strength, consumption, etc., in our reckoning.

Imagine two equal areas of land, one yielding five and the other ten. If the first area's inhabitants consume four, and the second's consume nine, the first leaves a surplus of one fifth of its produce and the second a surplus of one tenth. The ratio between these surpluses is therefore the reverse of the ratio between the yields. The land producing only five gives a surplus proportion twice that of the land producing ten.

But a doubled yield is not the issue here. Nor, I think, would anyone generally rank the fertility of cold countries equal to that of hot ones. Still, let us assume they are equal: put England on a level with Sicily, if you wish, and Poland with Egypt. Farther south we have Africa and the Indies; farther north, nothing at all. What different amounts of cultivation are needed to obtain this equal yield: in Sicily one need only scratch the earth; in England, how hard men must work! Where more hands are required to produce the same amount, the surplus must necessarily be smaller.

Remember, too, that an equal number of men consume far less in hot countries. For the sake of health, the climate demands moderation; Europeans who try to live there as they do at home all die of dysentery and indigestion. "We are," says Chardin, "carnivorous animals, wolves, in comparison with the Asiatics. Some attribute the sobriety of the Persians to the fact that their country is less cultivated; but it is my belief that their country abounds less in commodities because the inhabitants need less. If their frugality," he goes on, "were the effect of the nakedness of the land, only the poor would eat little; but everybody does so. Again, less or more would be eaten in various provinces, according to the land's fertility; but the same sobriety is found throughout the kingdom. They are very proud of their manner of life, saying that you have only to look at their hue to recognise how far it excels that of the Christians. In fact, the Persians are of an even hue; their skins are fair, fine and smooth; while the hue of their subjects, the Armenians, who live after the European fashion, is rough and blotchy, and their bodies are gross and unwieldy."

As you approach the equator, people live on less and less. They scarcely eat meat; their everyday food is rice, maize, curcur, millet and cassava. Millions in the Indies live on less than a halfpenny a day. Even within Europe the appetite of Northern peoples differs greatly from that of Southern peoples. A German's dinner would feed a Spaniard for a week. Where people eat more greedily, luxury accordingly takes the form of consumption. English luxury means a generously laden table; in Italy the feast consists of sugar and flowers.

Dress displays comparable differences in luxury. Where seasons change suddenly and sharply, people wear better but simpler clothing. Where dress serves only as decoration, appearance matters more than usefulness, and clothing itself becomes a luxury. In Naples you can see men walking in the Pausilippeum every day wearing gold-embroidered outer garments and nothing underneath. Buildings follow the same pattern: where the air poses no threat, magnificence is all that matters. In Paris and London you want a warm, comfortable home. In Madrid you have splendid salons, but not a single window that shuts, and your bedroom is a mere hole.

Food in hot countries is much more nourishing and full of juice; this third difference must affect the second. Why do Italians eat so many vegetables? Because theirs are good, nutritious and delicious. French vegetables, fed on water alone, offer little nourishment and receive little respect at table. Yet they occupy just as much land and take at least as much work to grow. It has been proved that Barbary wheat, though otherwise inferior to French wheat, produces much more flour. French wheat in turn produces more than wheat from northern countries. We may infer that this same progression generally holds as we move from the equator towards the pole. Is it not plainly a disadvantage if the same amount of produce contains less nourishment?

One further point both follows from all these considerations and reinforces them. Hot countries have less need of inhabitants than cold ones, yet can sustain more. This creates a double surplus, entirely to despotism's advantage. The wider the territory occupied by a given population, the harder it is to revolt. People cannot act together quickly or secretly, while government can readily uncover their plans and sever communications. But when a large population lives close together, government has less chance of taking the Sovereign's place. The people's leaders can deliberate in their homes as safely as the prince in his council, and crowds can assemble in the squares as quickly as his troops in their quarters. Tyrannical government therefore gains by acting across great distances. Through the rallying-points it establishes, its strength increases with distance, like a lever's.[1] The people's strength, by contrast, works only when concentrated. Disperse it and it vanishes, like gunpowder scattered on the ground, catching fire one grain at a time. The countries with the fewest inhabitants are therefore best suited to tyranny: savage beasts rule only in deserts.

As for the disadvantages of large States, our subject then was the government's authority over its own members; here it is the force it can use against its subjects. Its widely dispersed members give it rallying-points from which to act against distant populations. But it has no such rallying-point for acting directly on those members themselves. Thus the lever's length makes it weak in one case and strong in the other.

chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 9 — The Marks of a Good Government
paragraphs: The question "What absolutely is the best government?" is both undefined and impossible to answer. Or rather, there are as many valid answers as there are possible combinations of nations' absolute and relative circumstances.
It is quite another matter to ask what sign tells us whether a particular people is governed well or badly. That is a question of fact, and an answer is possible.

Yet no answer is agreed, because everyone insists on answering in his own way. Subjects praise public tranquillity; citizens praise individual liberty. One group wants possessions secured, the other wants persons secured. One calls the strictest government best, the other the mildest. One asks for crimes to be punished, the other for crimes to be prevented. One wants neighbouring countries to fear the State, the other would rather they paid it no attention. One is satisfied when money circulates, the other demands bread for the people. Even if agreement were reached on these and similar points, would that take us any further? Moral qualities cannot be measured precisely. Agreeing on the sign to look for does not mean agreeing on the value to give it.

For my part, I am constantly amazed that people fail to recognise so simple a sign, or are dishonest enough to deny it. What is political association for? To preserve its members and enable them to prosper. What most reliably shows that they survive and prosper? Their numbers: the size of the population. Look no farther, then, for the disputed sign. Other things being equal, the best government is unquestionably the one under which citizens increase and multiply most, without outside help, naturalisation or colonies. The worst is the government under which a people dwindles and declines. You who calculate must now do the counting, measuring and comparing.[1]

Human prosperity deserves the preference. Too much admiration has been given to ages in which literature and the arts flourished, because their cultivation's hidden purpose has not been understood and its fatal consequences have been overlooked. "Idque apud imperitos humanitas vocabatur, cum pars servitutis esset." ["Fools called 'humanity' what was a part of slavery," Tacitus, _Agricola_, 31.] Will we never recognise the ordinary self-interest behind the maxims that authors put into books? No: whatever they say, if a country loses its population despite its fame, all is not well. A poet's income of 100,000 francs is not enough to make his age the best of all. We should attend less to rulers' apparent peace and tranquillity than to the welfare of their nations as a whole, especially the most populous States. A hail-storm devastates several cantons, but seldom causes a famine. Uprisings and civil wars shake rulers severely, but they are not peoples' true misfortunes. A people may even enjoy a breathing-space while contenders dispute who will tyrannise over it. Its real prosperity or misery comes from its lasting condition. Decline sets in when the whole people stays crushed under the yoke, and rulers destroy it at will: "ubi solitudinem faciunt, pacem appellant" ["Where they create solitude, they call it peace," Tacitus, _Agricola_, 31.] When quarrels among the great troubled France, and the Coadjutor of Paris carried a dagger in his pocket to the Parliament, the French people still prospered and multiplied in dignity, comfort and freedom. Ancient Greece flourished amid the fiercest wars. Blood flowed in torrents, yet inhabitants covered the whole country. As Macchiavelli says, it seemed that our republic only prospered amid murder, proscription and civil war: its citizens' virtue, morality and independence strengthened it more than all their quarrels weakened it. A little unrest keeps the spirit resilient. What truly makes mankind prosper is liberty more than peace.

chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 10 — The Abuse of Government and Its Tendency to Degenerate
paragraphs: Just as the particular will constantly opposes the general will, government continually pushes against the Sovereignty. The stronger this pressure becomes, the more the constitution changes. Here no other corporate will exists to balance the prince's will by resisting it. Sooner or later, therefore, the prince inevitably suppresses the Sovereign and breaks the social treaty. This is the unavoidable defect built into the body politic. From the moment of its birth it works unceasingly towards its destruction, just as age and death eventually destroy the human body.
Government generally degenerates in two ways: _i.e._ it either contracts, or the State itself dissolves.

Government contracts when it moves from the many to the few: from democracy to aristocracy, and from aristocracy to royalty. This is its natural tendency.[1] If it moved backwards, from the few to the many, we could describe it as relaxing; but that reverse progression is impossible.

Governments change their form only when their energy is spent and they no longer have the strength to preserve what they possess. If a government simultaneously widened its scope and loosened its grip, its force would disappear altogether, and it would have still less chance of lasting. As the spring slackens, it must therefore be wound up and the hold tightened. Otherwise the State supported by it will collapse.
The State itself can dissolve in either of two different ways.

The first occurs when the prince stops administering the State according to law and seizes the Sovereign power. An extraordinary change follows: it is the State, rather than the government, that contracts. By this I mean that the great State dissolves, and a new one arises inside it, made up only of the government's members. To everyone else it is merely a master and a tyrant. The instant government takes the Sovereignty for itself, the social compact is therefore broken. Every private citizen regains his rightful natural liberty: force may compel his obedience, but no obligation binds him.

The same result follows when individual members of government take for themselves powers they should wield only collectively. This violates the laws just as seriously and creates even greater disorder. There are then, so to speak, as many princes as magistrates. The State is split as thoroughly as the government, and must either perish or take a different form.

When the State dissolves, whatever abuse of government has caused it is generally called _anarchy_. More specifically, democracy degenerates into _ochlocracy_, and aristocracy into _oligarchy_. I would also say that royalty degenerates into _tyranny_, but this last term has two meanings and needs explaining.

In everyday speech, a tyrant means a king who rules violently, disregarding law and justice. In the precise sense, however, a tyrant is someone who takes royal authority without any right to it. The Greeks understood "tyrant" in this way. They used it equally for good and bad princes whose authority lacked legitimacy.[2] In this sense _tyrant_ and _usurper_ mean exactly the same thing.

To give distinct things distinct names, I call someone who seizes royal authority a _tyrant_, and someone who seizes sovereign power a _despot_. The tyrant takes office against the laws in order to govern by them; the despot places himself above the laws themselves. Thus a tyrant cannot be a despot, whereas a despot is always a tyrant.

Its lagoons provide a striking example of this progression. Most remarkably, after existing for more than twelve hundred years, the Venetians still seem to occupy the second stage, reached with the _Serrar di Consiglio_ in 1198. The ancient Dukes sometimes cited against this argument were, it has been proved, in no sense Sovereigns, whatever the _Squittinio della libertà veneta_ may claim about them.

The Roman Republic will certainly be offered as an objection to my argument. People will say it took precisely the reverse path: from monarchy to aristocracy, then from aristocracy to democracy. That is by no means how I understand its history.

Romulus originally established a mixed government, which quickly sank into despotism. Particular causes brought the State to a premature death, as a newborn child may die before reaching adulthood. The Republic's true birth came with the expulsion of the Tarquins. At first, however, it had no settled form: by leaving the patriciate intact, it left its work half done. Hereditary aristocracy, the worst legitimate form of administration, consequently remained in conflict with democracy. As Macchiavelli has shown, the government acquired a definite form only when the tribunate was established. Only then did a real government and a genuine democracy exist. The people now served not merely as Sovereign but also as magistrate and judge. The senate was simply a subordinate tribunal, intended to moderate and concentrate the government. Even the consuls, though patricians, chief magistrates and commanders with absolute authority in war, were no more than presidents of the people within Rome itself.

From then on, government followed its natural tendency and moved strongly towards aristocracy. The patriciate, we might say, abolished itself. Aristocracy no longer resided in the patrician body, as at Venice and Genoa, but in the senate, whose members included both patricians and plebeians. It appeared even among the tribunes once they began taking an active governing role. Names do not change realities: whenever the people have rulers governing on their behalf, whatever those rulers are called, the government is an aristocracy.

Aristocracy's abuses produced the civil wars and the triumvirate. Sulla, Julius Cæsar and Augustus became monarchs in fact, and finally Tiberius's despotism dissolved the State. Rome's history therefore confirms the principle I have stated, rather than disproving it.

perpetua in ea civitate quæ libertate usa est (Cornelius Nepos, _Life of Miltiades_).
