[For all those are called and considered tyrants, who hold perpetual power in a State that has known liberty.] Aristotle does distinguish a tyrant from a king in the _Nicomachean Ethics_, Book viii, chapter x: the tyrant rules for his own benefit, the king solely for his subjects' good. But Greek authors generally used _tyrant_ in another sense, as Xenophon's _Hiero_ shows with particular clarity. Moreover, if we accepted Aristotle's distinction, we would have to conclude that since the world began there has never yet been a single king.

chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 11 — The Death of the Body Politic
paragraphs: Such is the natural and inevitable tendency of even the best-constituted governments. If Sparta and Rome perished, what State can hope to last forever? If we want to set up a long-lived form of government, let us not even dream of making it eternal. To succeed, we must not attempt the impossible, or flatter ourselves that we are giving the work of man a stability that human conditions do not allow.

The body politic, like the human body, begins to die as soon as it is born, and carries within itself the causes of its destruction. But each may have a constitution more or less robust, more or less suited to preserving it for a longer or shorter time. Man’s constitution is the work of nature; that of the State is the work of art. It is not in men’s power to prolong their own lives; but it is in their power to prolong the life of the State as much as possible, by giving it the best possible constitution. The best-constituted State will have an end; but it will end later than any other, unless some unforeseen accident brings about its untimely destruction.

The life-principle of the body politic lies in the sovereign authority. The legislative power is the heart of the State; the executive power is its brain, which sets all the parts in motion. The brain may be paralyzed and the individual still live. A man may remain an imbecile and live; but as soon as the heart stops performing its functions, the animal is dead.

The State exists by means not of the laws but of the legislative power. Yesterday’s law is not binding today; but silence is taken for tacit consent, and the Sovereign is held continually to confirm the laws it does not abrogate when it could. Whatever it has once declared itself to will, it wills always, unless it revokes its declaration.

Why, then, is so much respect paid to old laws? For this very reason. We must believe that nothing but the excellence of old acts of will can have preserved them so long: had the Sovereign not recognized them as wholesome throughout, it would have revoked them a thousand times. This is why, far from growing weak, the laws continually gain new strength in any well-constituted State; the precedent of antiquity makes them daily more venerable. Wherever, on the contrary, the laws grow weak as they grow old, this proves that there is no longer a legislative power, and that the State is dead.

chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 12 — How the Sovereign Authority Maintains Itself
paragraphs: The Sovereign has no force except its legislative power, so it can act only through laws. Since laws are nothing but authentic expressions of the general will, the Sovereign can act only while the people are assembled. I shall be told that an assembly of the people is an impossible fantasy. It is today; two thousand years ago it was not. Has human nature changed?

In moral affairs, the limits of what is possible are wider than we suppose. Our weaknesses, vices and prejudices are what narrow them. Petty souls cannot believe in great men; degraded slaves hear the word liberty and sneer.

Let what has actually been done show us what can be done. I shall leave aside the Republics of ancient Greece. But to my mind the Roman Republic was a great State, and Rome a great town. Its final census recorded four hundred thousand citizens fit to bear arms in Rome. The last reckoning of the Empire's population counted more than four million citizens, without including subjects, foreigners, women, children or slaves.

Think of the difficulties one might expect in frequently assembling the enormous population of that capital and its surroundings. Yet hardly a few weeks went by without the Roman people meeting, often several times. They exercised not only the rights of Sovereignty but some rights of government as well. They conducted certain kinds of business and decided certain legal cases. This entire people appeared in the public meeting-place almost as often in the capacity of magistrates as in that of citizens.

If we traced nations back to their earliest history, we would find similar councils in most ancient governments, even monarchies such as the Macedonian and the Frankish. At any rate, the single indisputable fact I have cited answers every objection about difficulty. It is sound reasoning to infer what is possible from what has actually happened.

chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 13 — The Same (continued)
paragraphs: It is not enough that the people once assembled and settled the State's constitution by approving a body of laws. Nor is it enough to have established a permanent government, or made arrangements once and for all for electing magistrates. Unforeseen events may require extraordinary assemblies; besides these, there must be regular assemblies on fixed dates, which no one can cancel or postpone. On the appointed day the law itself legitimately calls the people together, without any need for a formal summons.

Apart from assemblies authorised simply by their appointed date, however, a popular assembly is unlawful unless the magistrates charged with that duty summon it in the prescribed manner. All acts of such an unlawful gathering must be considered void, since the command to assemble must itself come from the law.

How often lawful assemblies should meet depends on too many circumstances for exact rules to be possible. We can say only this in general: the stronger the government becomes, the more frequently the Sovereign ought to appear.

That may work for one town, I shall be told; but what if several towns make up the State? Must sovereign authority be divided among them? Or must it be gathered into one town, with every other town placed under its rule?

My answer is: neither. First, sovereign authority forms a single, simple whole; dividing it destroys it. Second, one town can no more legitimately be subjected to another than one nation can. The body politic exists essentially to reconcile liberty with obedience. Subject and Sovereign are corresponding terms referring to the same people, and their two ideas come together in the single word "citizen."

I add that combining several towns in a single city is always bad. If we choose to make that union, we should not expect to escape its natural drawbacks. There is no point in confronting someone who wants only small States with abuses peculiar to large ones. But how can small States acquire the strength to withstand great powers, as the Greek towns once withstood the Great King, and Holland and Switzerland more recently withstood the House of Austria?

Still, if the State cannot be brought within the proper limits, one remedy remains. Let it have no capital. Move the seat of government from one town to another, and let the country's Provincial Estates assemble in each town in turn.

Distribute the population evenly across the territory, give the same rights everywhere, and bring life and abundance to every part. In this way the State will be as strong and as well governed as it can be. Remember that town walls are built from the wreckage of country homes. Whenever I see a palace rise in the capital, I picture an entire countryside laid waste.

chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 14 — The Same (continued)
paragraphs: As soon as the people lawfully assemble as a sovereign body, the government's jurisdiction ends altogether and executive power is suspended. The humblest citizen's person becomes as sacred and inviolable as the chief magistrate's. When the person represented is present, representatives cease to exist. Ignoring or forgetting this rule caused most of the disturbances in Rome's comitia. There the consuls were merely presidents of the people, the tribunes merely speakers,[1] and the senate had no standing at all.

The prince has always feared these periods of suspension, when he acknowledges, or ought to acknowledge, someone actually superior to himself. Popular assemblies protect the body politic and restrain government, and rulers have always dreaded them. They therefore spare no effort, objection, obstacle or promise that might prevent citizens from holding them. If citizens are greedy, cowardly and faint-hearted, preferring comfort to liberty, they do not resist the government's renewed efforts for long. As the force opposing these assemblies continually increases, sovereign authority finally vanishes. Thus most cities decline and perish before their proper time.
Sometimes, however, an intermediate power comes between sovereign authority and arbitrary government. We must say something about that power.
Parliament. These similar functions would have brought consuls and tribunes into conflict even if every form of jurisdiction had been suspended.

chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 15 — Deputies or Representatives
paragraphs: Once public service stops being the citizens' principal concern, and they prefer contributing money to serving in person, the State is close to ruin. If war requires them to march, they pay soldiers and remain at home. If a council must meet, they appoint deputies and remain at home. Their idleness and money finally provide them with soldiers who enslave their country and representatives who sell it.

The bustle of commerce and the arts, the selfish pursuit of profit, softness and a taste for comforts all encourage people to substitute payments for personal service. Men give up part of their profits to gain leisure in which to make more. Give money, and chains will soon follow. _Finance_ is a word belonging to slavery, unknown in the city-state. In a genuinely free country citizens do everything with their own hands and nothing through money. Far from paying to escape their duties, they would pay for the privilege of carrying them out themselves. My view is far from the usual one: I consider compulsory labour less hostile to liberty than taxation.

The better a State's constitution, the more public business takes precedence over private business in its citizens' minds. Private concerns even become much less important: the total common happiness supplies a larger share of each person's happiness, leaving him less to seek in his individual affairs. In a well-ordered city everyone hurries to the assemblies. Under bad government no one will take a step towards them. People have no interest in what happens there; they know the general will will not prevail; and, finally, domestic concerns absorb all their attention. Good laws produce better laws, while bad laws produce worse ones. Once anyone says of the State's affairs, _What does it matter to me?_ we may give the State up for lost.

Weak patriotism, vigorous private interests, the enormous size of States, conquest and governmental abuses gave rise to the practice of sending deputies or representatives of the people to national assemblies. In some countries people have presumed to name these the Third Estate. Thus two orders' particular interests take first and second place, while the public interest comes only third.

Sovereignty cannot be represented for the same reason that it cannot be alienated. Its essence is the general will, and a will cannot have a representative: it is either that very will or a different one; nothing lies between. The people's deputies therefore are not, and cannot be, its representatives. They are only its stewards and cannot make any final decision. A law that the people have not personally ratified is void--indeed, it is no law at all. The English people think themselves free, but are gravely mistaken. They are free only while electing members of parliament. Once those members are elected, the people become slaves and count for nothing. Indeed, their use of those brief moments of liberty shows that they deserve to lose them.

Representation is a modern idea, inherited from feudal government--that unjust and absurd system which degrades humanity and dishonours the very name of man. In ancient republics, and even monarchies, the people had no representatives; the term itself was unknown. Rome provides a remarkable instance. Although the tribunes were so sacred, no one even imagined that they might take over the people's functions. Surrounded by that enormous multitude, they never tried to enact a single plebiscitum on their own authority. Yet we can glimpse the difficulties such numbers sometimes caused from events under the Gracchi, when some citizens had to vote from the rooftops.

Where liberty and right mean everything, inconvenience means nothing. This wise people valued everything properly. It allowed its lictors to do things its tribunes would never have dared attempt, because it had no fear that the lictors would claim to represent it.

To understand how the tribunes sometimes did represent the people, we need only consider how government represents the Sovereign. Law is simply a declaration of the general will, so the people plainly cannot be represented when exercising legislative power. Executive power, however, is only the force used to put law into effect. In exercising that power the people both can and should have representatives. A close examination would therefore show us that very few nations possess any laws. However that may be, the tribunes certainly had no executive power. The powers entrusted to them could never entitle them to represent the Roman people; they could do so only by seizing the senate's powers.

In Greece the people did for themselves everything they needed to do, and were continually assembled in the public square. They enjoyed a mild climate, had no natural greed, and left their work to slaves; liberty was their chief concern. Without those advantages, how can you preserve the same rights? Your harsher climates increase your needs.[1] For half the year you cannot occupy your public squares. Your languages are too flat to carry in the open air. You sacrifice more for profit than for liberty, and poverty frightens you more than slavery.

What follows? Can liberty survive only with slavery's assistance? Perhaps it can. Extremes meet. Everything outside the course of nature has its disadvantages, and civil society has more than anything else. In certain unhappy circumstances we can preserve our freedom only at others' expense: the citizen can be wholly free only when the slave is most completely enslaved. Sparta was such a case. You modern peoples have no slaves, but are yourselves slaves; you buy their liberty with your own. You boast of preferring this arrangement, but to no purpose: I see more cowardice in it than humanity.

None of this means that slaves are necessary, or that a right to slavery is legitimate. I am simply explaining why modern peoples, though they think themselves free, have representatives, whereas ancient peoples did not. In any event, as soon as a people consents to representation, its freedom ends: it no longer exists.

Taking everything together, I cannot see how the Sovereign can continue to exercise its rights among us unless the city is very small. But will a very small city not be conquered? No. Later I shall explain how a great people's external strength[2] can be joined to the manageable political organisation and sound order of a small State.
To wish to submit to its chains is, in our case, to bend under them far more inevitably than in theirs.
While discussing external relations, I reached the question of confederations. This subject is entirely new, and its principles remain to be established.

chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 16 — That the Institution of Government Is Not a Contract
paragraphs: Once the legislative power has been firmly established, the next thing is to establish the executive power in the same way; for the executive power, which operates only by particular acts, is not of the essence of the legislative, and is naturally separate from it. If it were possible for the Sovereign, as such, to possess the executive power, right and fact would be so confused that no one could tell what was law and what was not; and the body politic, thus disfigured, would soon fall prey to the very violence it was instituted to prevent.

Since the citizens, by the social contract, are all equal, all can prescribe what all should do, but no one has a right to demand that another do what he himself does not. It is precisely this right — indispensable for giving the body politic life and movement — that the Sovereign, in instituting the government, confers upon the prince.

It has been held that this act of establishment was a contract between the people and the rulers it sets over itself — a contract laying down terms binding one side to command and the other to obey. This is, I am sure it will be admitted, an odd kind of contract to enter into. But let us see whether this view can be maintained.

First, the supreme authority can no more be modified than it can be alienated; to limit it is to destroy it. It is absurd and self-contradictory for the Sovereign to set a superior over itself; to bind itself to obey a master would be a return to absolute liberty.

Moreover, it is clear that this contract between the people and certain particular persons would be a particular act; and from this it follows that it can be neither a law nor an act of Sovereignty, and so would be illegitimate.

It is also plain that the contracting parties, in relation to each other, would be under the law of nature alone, with no guarantees of their mutual undertakings — a position completely at odds with the civil state. Since the man who has force at his command is always in a position to control execution, it would come to the same thing if we called a “contract” the act of one man saying to another, “I give you all my goods, on condition that you give me back as much of them as you please.”

There is only one contract in the State — the act of association — and that contract in itself excludes the existence of a second. It is impossible to conceive of any public contract that would not be a violation of the first.

chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 17 — The Institution of Government
paragraphs: Under what general category, then, should we place the act that establishes government? Let me begin by saying that this is a compound act, consisting of two others: first the enactment of the law, then its execution.
In the first act the Sovereign decrees that a governing body of a specified form shall exist. Plainly this decree is a law.

In the second act the people appoint the rulers entrusted with this newly established government. Because an appointment is a particular act, it plainly does not constitute another law. It merely follows from the first law and exercises a governmental function.

The difficulty is to see how government can perform an act before it exists, and how the people, whose position is either Sovereign or subject, can in certain circumstances become a prince or magistrate.

Here we discover one of the body politic's astonishing properties: its ability to reconcile operations that seem contradictory. Sovereignty suddenly converts itself into a democratic government. Without any perceptible change, simply through a new relation of everyone to everyone else, citizens become magistrates. They move from general acts to particular ones, from making laws to putting them into effect.

This change of relationship is not an ingenious abstraction with no practical examples. It happens daily in the English Parliament. On certain occasions the Lower House turns itself into Grand Committee to discuss business more effectively. One moment it is a sovereign court; the next it is merely a commission. Afterwards, as the House of Commons, it receives its own report of proceedings in Grand Committee and debates again under one name what it has already decided under another.

Democratic government has this special advantage: a simple act of the general will can bring it into actual existence. This provisional government then either stays in office, if that form is chosen, or establishes, on the Sovereign's behalf, the government prescribed by law. The entire procedure is thus regular. No other way of establishing government can be legitimate or consistent with the principles we have laid down so far.

chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 18 — How to Check the Usurpations of Government
paragraphs: Our discussion confirms Chapter XVI and makes the position clear. Establishing government is an act of law, not a contract. Those entrusted with executive power are the people's officers, not their masters; the people may appoint and dismiss them whenever they choose. These officers have no contract to negotiate: their task is obedience. In taking up the functions the State assigns them, they are simply performing their duties as citizens. They have not the slightest right to bargain over the conditions on which they will serve.

Thus when the people establish hereditary government--whether a monarchy restricted to one family or an aristocracy restricted to one class--they make no binding promise. They merely give the administration a provisional form, lasting until they choose to arrange it differently.

Such changes are certainly always dangerous. An established government should never be disturbed unless it becomes incompatible with the public good. But the caution required here is a rule of prudence, not a principle of right. The State is no more obliged to leave civil authority with its rulers than it is to leave military authority with its generals.

It is also true that we cannot take too much care in observing every formality needed on these occasions. These distinguish a regular, lawful act from a seditious disturbance, and the will of the whole people from a faction's shouting. Here above all, the unwelcome possibility must receive no concession beyond what the strictest reasoning makes impossible to deny. This requirement greatly helps the prince keep power against the people's wishes without anyone being able to call him a usurper. Apparently exercising only his rights, he finds it easy to enlarge them. Under the excuse of preserving peace he prevents assemblies intended to restore order. He then exploits a silence he forbids anyone to break, or irregularities he himself provokes. He claims the support of those whom fear keeps silent, and punishes those bold enough to speak. That is how the decemvirs, elected first for one year and retained for a second, tried to make their power permanent by forbidding the comitia to meet. Through this simple device, every government in the world, once invested with public power, eventually takes sovereign authority for itself.

The regular assemblies I have already described are meant to prevent or delay this disaster, especially when they require no formal summons. In that case the prince cannot prevent them without openly revealing himself as a violator of the law and an enemy of the State.
These assemblies exist solely to preserve the social treaty. They should always open with two propositions that cannot be withheld from the meeting, and each proposition must receive a separate vote.
The first proposition asks: "Does it please the Sovereign to preserve the present form of government?"
The second proposition asks: "Does it please the people to leave its administration in the hands of those who are actually in charge of it?"

Here I assume what I believe I have demonstrated: no fundamental law in the State is beyond repeal, not even the social compact itself. If every citizen unanimously assembled to dissolve that compact, there can be no doubt that its dissolution would be entirely legitimate. Grotius goes further: he believes each man may leave his State, renounce membership of it, and recover his natural liberty and his possessions.[1] It would indeed be absurd if all citizens assembled together lacked a power that each could exercise alone.
Nor may he evade the duty of serving his country in its hour of need. To flee then would be a punishable crime: it would amount to desertion, rather than withdrawal.

chapters.title: Book 4, Chapter 1 — That the General Will Is Indestructible
paragraphs: As long as several men in assembly regard themselves as a single body, they have only a single will, concerned with their common preservation and general well-being. In this case, all the springs of the State are vigorous and simple, and its rules clear and luminous; there are no entanglements or conflicts of interest; the common good is everywhere plainly visible, and only good sense is needed to see it. Peace, unity, and equality are the enemies of political subtleties. Men who are upright and simple are hard to deceive precisely because of their simplicity; lures and ingenious pretexts fail to take them in, and they are not even cunning enough to be dupes. When, among the happiest people in the world, bands of peasants are seen regulating affairs of State under an oak, and always acting wisely, can we help despising the elaborate methods of other nations, which make themselves illustrious and miserable with so much art and mystery?

A State so governed needs very few laws; and when new ones become necessary, the necessity is universally seen. The first man to propose them merely says what everyone has already felt, and there is no question of factions, intrigues, or eloquence to push into law what each has already decided to do, as soon as he is sure the rest will join him.

Theorists are led astray because, seeing only States that have been wrongly constituted from the start, they are struck by the impossibility of applying such a policy to them. They make great sport of all the absurdities that a clever rascal or an insinuating speaker might persuade the people of Paris or London to believe. They do not realize that Cromwell would have been put to “the bells” by the people of Berne, and the Duc de Beaufort on the treadmill by the Genevese.

But when the social bond begins to loosen and the State to grow weak, when particular interests begin to make themselves felt and the smaller societies start to influence the larger, the common interest changes and meets opponents; opinion is no longer unanimous; the general will ceases to be the will of all; contradictory views and debates arise; and the best advice is no longer accepted without question.

Finally, when the State, on the brink of ruin, maintains only a vain, illusory, and formal existence, when in every heart the social bond is broken, and the meanest interest brazenly seizes the sacred name of “public good,” the general will falls silent. All men, guided by secret motives, no more give their views as citizens than if the State had never existed; and iniquitous decrees, aimed solely at private interest, are passed under the name of laws.

Does it follow that the general will has been wiped out or corrupted? Not at all: it is always constant, unalterable, and pure; but it is subordinated to other wills that encroach on its sphere. Each man, in detaching his interest from the common interest, sees clearly that he cannot entirely separate them; but his share in the public misfortunes seems negligible to him beside the exclusive good he aims at making his own. Apart from this particular good, he wills the general good in his own interest as strongly as anyone else. Even in selling his vote for money, he does not extinguish the general will in himself — he only evades it. The fault he commits is changing the question, and answering something different from what he is asked. Instead of saying, by his vote, “It is to the State’s advantage,” he says, “It is to this or that man’s or party’s advantage that this or that view should prevail.” So the law of public order in assemblies is not so much to maintain the general will in them as to ensure that the question is always put to it, and the answer always given by it.

I could here set down many reflections on the simple right of voting in every act of Sovereignty — a right no one can take from the citizens — and also on the right to state views, make proposals, divide and discuss, which the government is always most careful to leave only to its own members; but this important subject would need a treatise of its own, and one cannot say everything in a single work.

chapters.title: Book 4, Chapter 2 — Voting
paragraphs: The previous chapter shows that the conduct of public business can reveal quite clearly both the people's moral condition and the body politic's health. The greater the agreement within assemblies--in other words, the closer opinions come to unanimity--the more firmly the general will prevails. Long arguments, divisions and uproar, by contrast, announce that particular interests have gained control and the State is declining.

This seems less obvious where the constitution contains two or more orders, as Rome's did with patricians and plebeians. Their disputes often disrupted the comitia even during the Republic's finest days. Yet the exception is more apparent than real. The body politic's inherent defect then produced, so to speak, two States within one. What fails to hold for the two together holds for each considered separately. Even in the stormiest periods, the people's plebiscita passed peacefully and by large majorities whenever the Senate left them alone. Since the citizens shared a single interest, the people had a single will.

At the circle's opposite extreme, unanimity appears again: citizens reduced to servitude have lost both their liberty and their will. Fear and flattery turn voting into applause. Deliberation ends, leaving only adoration or curses. This was the senate's degrading way of expressing itself under the Emperors, sometimes with absurd precautions. Tacitus tells us that under Otho, the senators heaped curses on Vitellius while deliberately raising a deafening noise. If Vitellius ever became their master, they hoped he would be unable to tell what each had said.

These different considerations determine the rules for counting votes and weighing opinions. Those rules must vary with the ease or difficulty of discovering the general will, and with how far the State has declined.

Only one law, by its very nature, requires everyone's consent: the social compact. Entering civil association is the most voluntary of all acts. Every man is born free and master of himself. No one, on any pretext whatever, can subject him without his consent. To declare that a slave's son is born a slave is to declare that he is not born a man.

If some people object when the social compact is formed, their objection does not invalidate it; it simply excludes them from it. They remain foreigners among citizens. Once the State is established, living there amounts to consent: to reside within its territory is to submit to the Sovereign.[1]

Except for this original contract, a majority vote always binds everyone else; the contract itself establishes that rule. But people ask how a man can remain free while being compelled to obey wills other than his own. How can dissenters be free and yet subject to laws they never approved?

I reply that this puts the question wrongly. A citizen consents to every law, including laws passed over his objections, and even laws that punish him when he dares to break them. The enduring will of all the State's members is the general will; it makes them citizens and free.[2] When a law is proposed to the popular assembly, the question is not precisely whether people approve or reject it. They are asked whether it agrees with the general will, which is their own will. Every voter expresses his judgment on that point, and counting the votes reveals the general will. If an opinion opposed to mine wins, that proves simply that I was mistaken: what I took for the general will was not the general will. Had my particular opinion prevailed, I would have brought about the opposite of what I willed. In that case, it is I who would not have been free.
This does, of course, assume that the majority still possesses every quality of the general will. Once it loses them, liberty becomes impossible, whichever side a man supports.

When I earlier showed how particular wills replace the general will in public deliberations, I sufficiently indicated practical ways to prevent the abuse. I shall return to them later. I also set out the principles for determining the proportion of votes needed to declare that will. One vote's difference breaks a tie; one opponent breaks unanimity. Between equality and unanimity, however, lie many degrees of unequal division. The required proportion may be set at any of them, according to the body politic's condition and needs.

Two general rules can guide this proportion. First, the more serious and important the question, the closer the winning opinion should come to unanimity. Second, the greater the need for speed, the smaller the required margin of votes may be. Where a decision has to be reached without any delay, a majority of just one vote should be sufficient. The first rule seems better suited to laws, the second to practical business. In every case, combining the two gives the best proportion for deciding what majority is needed.

Elsewhere, family ties, possessions, the absence of a refuge, necessity or force may keep a man in a country against his wishes. His residence there then no longer proves, by itself, that he consents either to the contract or to its violation.

On prisons and on the chains worn by galley-slaves, this use of the device is right and just. Only wrongdoers, of whatever rank, prevent citizens from being free. A country that put all such men in the galleys would enjoy the most perfect liberty.

chapters.title: Book 4, Chapter 3 — Elections
paragraphs: There are two ways to elect the prince and the magistrates--acts which, as I have said, are compound in nature. They may be selected by choice or by lot. Various republics have used both methods, and Venice still elects its Doge through an extremely complicated combination of the two.

"Election by lot," says Montesquieu, "is democratic in nature." I accept that, but what does it mean? "The lot," he goes on, "is a way of making choice that is unfair to nobody; it leaves each citizen a reasonable hope of serving his country." This does not explain the reason.

Remember that choosing rulers belongs to government, not to Sovereignty. We can then understand why selection by lot is more natural to democracy: in a democracy administration improves as the number of acts it performs decreases.

In a true democracy, being a magistrate is a demanding duty, not a benefit. It cannot justly be imposed on one person rather than another. Only the law can place that burden on whoever draws the lot. Everyone then faces the same conditions, and no human will determines the choice. No particular application therefore changes the law's universal character.
Under aristocracy, the prince selects the prince; government perpetuates itself. Election by vote is therefore the proper arrangement.

The election of Venice's Doge supports this distinction instead of disproving it: a mixed procedure suits a mixed government. It is a mistake to call Venice a true aristocracy. Although the people have no part in government, the nobility itself constitutes the people. Numerous poor Barnabotes never come close to holding office; their nobility consists only of the empty title of Excellency and a seat in the Great Council. That council has as many members as our General Council at Geneva, and its illustrious members enjoy no greater privileges than our ordinary citizens. Despite the immense difference between the two republics, Geneva's _bourgeoisie_ unquestionably corresponds exactly to Venice's _patriciate_. Our _natives_ and _inhabitants_ correspond to Venice's _townsmen_ and _people_; our _peasants_ to its mainland _subjects_. However one views that republic, once its size is set aside, its government is no more aristocratic than ours. The entire difference is that we have no ruler for life, and therefore no need, as Venice has, to draw lots.

In a true democracy, selection by lot would have few drawbacks. Equality would prevail everywhere--in morals and abilities as well as principles and wealth--so it would scarcely matter who was chosen. But, as I have already said, true democracy exists only as an ideal.

Where choice and lot are used together, choice should fill posts requiring special abilities, such as military commands. The lot suits offices, such as judgeships, for which sound judgment, justice and integrity are sufficient. In a properly constituted State, every citizen possesses these qualities.

Monarchical government has no place for either voting or drawing lots. The monarch is by right the sole prince and sole magistrate; only he may choose his lieutenants. When the Abbé de Saint-Pierre proposed increasing the number of the King of France's Councils and electing their members by ballot, he failed to see that he was proposing a change in the form of government.

I should now discuss how opinions are expressed and counted in the people's assembly. But an account of this part of Rome's constitution may illustrate all the rules I could offer more forcefully. A thoughtful reader will find it worthwhile to follow in some detail how a Council of two hundred thousand men conducted both public and private business.

chapters.title: Book 4, Chapter 4 — The Roman Comitia
paragraphs: We have no thoroughly reliable records of Rome's earliest period. Indeed, most accounts of it are very probably fables. In general, the most instructive part of a people's history--the story of its foundation--is also the part we know least about. Daily experience teaches us the causes of revolutions in empires. But since new peoples are no longer being formed, we have scarcely anything beyond conjecture to explain how they first came into being.

Established customs at least prove that those customs began somewhere. Among traditions reaching back to their origins, we should regard as most reliable those supported by the greatest authorities and the strongest evidence. I have tried to follow these rules in investigating how the world's freest and most powerful people exercised its supreme authority.

After Rome was founded, the infant republic--that is, its founder's army, made up of Albans, Sabines and foreigners--was separated into three classes. This division gave them the name _tribes_. Each tribe contained ten _curiæ_; each _curia_ was further divided into _decuriæ_. Their leaders were called _curiones_ and _decuriones_.

In addition, each tribe supplied a body of one hundred _Equites_, or Knights, known as a _century_. These divisions were unnecessary in a town, which shows that they were originally military only. Yet an instinct for greatness seems to have prompted Rome, while still a little township, to equip itself in advance with a political system fit for the world's capital.

This first division soon created a difficulty. The Alban tribe (Ramnenses) and the Sabine tribe (Tatienses) remained unchanged, while the foreigners' tribe (Luceres) kept growing as more foreigners settled in Rome. It soon became stronger than the others. Servius corrected this dangerous imbalance by changing the basis of division. He abolished the racial distinction and substituted one based on the district in which each tribe lived. He replaced the three tribes with four, each occupying and taking its name from one of Rome's hills. This both corrected the existing inequality and guarded against future problems. To make the division apply to persons as well as places, he prohibited inhabitants from moving between districts, thereby preventing the races from mixing.

He also doubled the three existing centuries of Knights and added twelve more, while preserving the old names. This straightforward, prudent measure distinguished the body of Knights from the people without provoking a murmur from them.

Besides the four urban tribes, Servius established fifteen rural tribes, so called because their members lived in the countryside, divided into fifteen cantons. Fifteen more were later created. The Roman people ultimately had thirty-five tribes, and that division lasted until the Republic ended.

The separation of urban and rural tribes produced an effect worth noting, both because it has no parallel elsewhere and because Rome owed to it the preservation of her morals and the growth of her empire. One might expect the urban tribes soon to seize all power and honours, and quickly discredit the rural tribes. Precisely the opposite happened. Everyone knows the early Romans' fondness for country life. They owed it to their wise founder, who associated agricultural and military labour with liberty, while, so to speak, assigning arts, crafts, intrigue, wealth and slavery to the town.

All Rome's most distinguished citizens thus lived in the fields and cultivated the soil. People became accustomed to looking there alone for the republic's supports. Since the best patricians lived this way, everyone honoured it. They preferred the villager's simple, hardworking life to the laziness and idleness of Rome's _bourgeoisie_. A man who would have been a miserable proletarian in town became a respected citizen by working the land. As Varro says, our noble-minded ancestors had good reason to make the village a nursery for the hardy, brave men who defended them in war and fed them in peace. Pliny explicitly says that the rural tribes were honoured for the men they contained. Cowards whom people wanted to disgrace, by contrast, were publicly transferred to urban tribes. The Sabine Appius Claudius received honours in abundance when he settled at Rome, and was enrolled in a rural tribe that later bore his family name. Finally, freedmen always joined urban tribes, never rural ones. Throughout the Republic there is not a single example of a freedman reaching any magistracy, even after becoming a citizen.
This was an excellent rule, but it was pushed so far that eventually it changed the political system and certainly introduced an abuse.

First, after long claiming the right to move citizens from one tribe to another at their own discretion, the censors allowed most people to enrol in whichever tribe they wished. This permission certainly did no good, and also deprived the censorship of one of its strongest instruments. Furthermore, the rich and powerful all enrolled in rural tribes, while freedmen who had gained citizenship stayed with the populace in urban ones. Both kinds of tribe soon lost their connection to any particular place or territory. Everything became so confused that only the registers could identify which tribe someone belonged to. _Tribe_ now denoted persons instead of a territorial reality--or, rather, became little more than a fiction.
The urban tribes also had the advantage of being close at hand, and therefore often dominated the comitia. They sold the State to anyone who stooped to buy the votes of the rabble that composed them.

The founder had given each tribe ten _curiæ_. The whole Roman people, then living within the walls, therefore comprised thirty _curia_. Each had its own temples, gods, officers, priests and festivals. These festivals, called _compitalia_, corresponded to the _paganalia_ that the rural tribes held in later times.

When Servius introduced his new division, thirty _curiæ_ could not be distributed equally among four tribes. Unwilling to alter them, he left them as a separate division of Rome's inhabitants, entirely independent of the tribes. The rural tribes and their members, however, had no _curiæ_. Tribes had by then become a purely civil institution. A new method of raising troops also made Romulus's military divisions unnecessary. Consequently every citizen belonged to a tribe, but very many citizens belonged to no _curia_.

Servius introduced a third division as well, separate from the other two, and its consequences made it the most important. He arranged the entire Roman people in six classes, based on wealth rather than residence or personal identity. The rich occupied the first classes, the poor the last, and people of moderate means those between. These six classes were further divided into one hundred and ninety-three bodies called centuries. Their distribution gave the first class alone more than half the centuries, and the last only one. Thus the class with the fewest members contained the most centuries, while the whole final class counted as a single subdivision, although it included more than half of Rome's inhabitants.

To make the consequences of this arrangement less apparent to the people, Servius gave it a military appearance. He assigned two centuries of armourers to the second class and two of makers of instruments of war to the fourth. In every class except the last, he separated young men from old: those required to bear arms from those whose age legally exempted them. This distinction, more than differences in wealth, made frequent censuses or counts necessary. Finally, he required the assembly to meet in the Campus Martius, and ordered everyone of military age to attend armed.

He did not separate young and old in the last class because its members, the populace, had no right to bear arms for their country. To acquire the right to defend a hearth, a man first had to possess a hearth of his own. Of all the troops of beggars who now lend splendour to kings' armies, perhaps not one would have escaped contemptuous expulsion from a Roman cohort in the days when soldiers defended liberty.

Even in this last class, however, a distinction separated _proletarians_ from _capite censi._ The former had not lost quite everything: they at least supplied citizens to the State and, in urgent need, sometimes soldiers. Those possessing nothing, countable only as heads, were considered utterly worthless. Marius was the first to lower himself to enlisting them.

Without deciding here whether this third arrangement was good or bad in itself, I think I can say what alone made it workable: the early Romans' simple morals, lack of self-interest, love of farming, and contempt for commerce and the pursuit of profit. Among what modern people could such a system last twenty years without overturning the State, amid consuming greed, unrest, intrigue, constant changes of residence and perpetual shifts in fortune? We must remember that Rome's morals and censorship were stronger than this institution and corrected its defects. A rich man who displayed his wealth too ostentatiously found himself demoted to the poor class.

All this readily explains why people almost always speak of five classes, although there were six. The sixth supplied neither soldiers to the army nor votes in the Campus Martius.[1] With almost no function in the State, it was seldom thought worth counting.

These, then, were the different divisions of the Roman people. Now consider their effect on the assemblies. Lawfully summoned assemblies were called _comitia_. They usually met in Rome's public square or the Campus Martius, and were named _Comitia Curiata, Comitia Centuriata_, or _Comitia Tributa_ according to the division used to convene them. Romulus founded the _Comitia Curiata_, Servius the _Centuriata_, and the people's tribunes the _Tributa_. No law was approved and no magistrate elected outside the comitia. Since every citizen belonged to a _curia_, a century or a tribe, every citizen possessed the right to vote. The Roman people were therefore truly sovereign both _de jure_ and _de facto_.

Three conditions made a meeting of the comitia lawful and gave its acts legal force. First, the body or magistrate calling it had to hold the required authority. Second, it had to meet on a legally permitted day. Third, the auguries had to be favourable.

The first rule explains itself; the second concerns policy. Comitia could not meet on festivals or market-days, when country people visiting Rome on business had no time to spend all day in the square. The third rule enabled the senate to check the proud, restless people and suitably curb seditious tribunes' enthusiasm. The tribunes, however, found several ways round this obstacle.

Questions about laws and the election of rulers were not the only matters submitted to the comitia for judgment. Since the Roman people had assumed government's most important functions, one might say that their assemblies settled the fate of Europe. The variety of their business produced different forms of assembly, depending on the matters requiring a decision.

A comparison is enough to assess these different forms. In establishing _curiæ_, Romulus intended the people to restrain the senate and the senate to restrain the people, while he remained superior to both. Through this assembly he gave the people the full authority of numbers, balancing the power and wealth he left with the patricians. Yet, in the spirit of monarchy, he still favoured the patricians: their clients' influence could secure a majority of votes. The admirable institution of patron and client was a masterpiece of statesmanship and humanity. Without it, the patriciate could not have survived its blatant conflict with the republican spirit. Rome alone deserves the honour of giving the world this great example. It never produced any abuse, and yet no one has ever followed it.
Assemblies by _curiæ_ continued under the kings until Servius's time, and the later Tarquin's reign was not recognised as legitimate. Royal laws were therefore generally known as _leges curiatæ_.

Under the Republic the _curiæ_ remained restricted to the four urban tribes and contained only Rome's populace. They suited neither the senate, which led the patricians, nor the tribunes, who, despite being plebeians, headed the prosperous citizens. The _curiæ_ consequently lost respect. Their decline went so far that thirty lictors would meet and perform the business properly belonging to the _Comitia Curiata_.

The division into centuries favoured aristocracy so strongly that at first it is hard to understand how the senate could ever lose in the comitia named after them. These assemblies elected consuls, censors and the other curule magistrates. Of the one hundred and ninety-three centuries distributed across the six classes of the Roman people, ninety-eight belonged to the first class. Since voting counted centuries alone, this one class held a majority over all the others together. If its centuries agreed, no further votes were even collected. The smallest number's decision counted as the multitude's. In the _Comitia Centuriata_, then, the size of men's purses determined decisions much more than the number of their votes.

Two things, however, limited this immense authority. First, the tribunes generally belonged to the wealthy class, and large numbers of plebeians always did. Within the first class they therefore balanced the patricians' influence.

The second limitation worked as follows. Rather than have every century vote in rank order, always starting with the first, the Romans drew one by lot to conduct the election alone. All the centuries were then summoned on a different day, in order of rank, to repeat the election and, usually, confirm it. In this way the power of setting an example passed from rank to the lot, in accordance with a democratic principle.

This practice had another benefit. Between the two elections, rural citizens could investigate the merits of the provisionally nominated candidate instead of voting without knowing the case. But the wish to speed proceedings served as a pretext for abolishing the custom, and the two elections came to be held on the same day.

The _Comitia Tributa_ were properly the Roman people's council. Only the tribunes summoned them; there the tribunes were elected and enacted their plebiscita. The senate had neither standing in these assemblies nor even a right to attend. Compelled to obey laws on which they could not vote, senators were in this respect less free than the humblest citizens. This injustice was thoroughly ill-judged, and by itself enough to invalidate decrees made by a body that excluded some of its own members. If all patricians had attended the comitia by their rights as citizens, they would have attended merely as private individuals. They could have had little influence in a vote counted by heads, where the lowliest proletarian counted as much as the _princeps senatus_.

We can therefore see that these different ways of dividing an enormous people and collecting its votes did more than create order. They were not interchangeable procedures, neutral in themselves. Each produced results connected to the purposes for which it had been preferred.

Without entering into further detail, we can conclude from this account that the _Comitia Tributa_ most favoured popular government, and the _Comitia Centuriata_ aristocracy. Rome's populace held the majority in the _Comitia Curiata_, which could serve only tyranny and wicked schemes. Those assemblies naturally fell into disrepute. Even agitators avoided a method that exposed their intentions too clearly. Unquestionably, the Roman people's full majesty resided only in the _Comitia Centuriata_, the one assembly including everyone. The _Comitia Curiata_ excluded the rural tribes, while the _Comitia Tributa_ excluded the senate and patricians.

The early Romans' voting procedure was as simple as their morals, though less simple than Sparta's. Each voter spoke his choice aloud and a clerk recorded it. A majority within each tribe decided that tribe's vote, and a majority of tribes decided the people's vote; _curiæ_ and centuries followed the same rule. This worked well while honesty prevailed and men were ashamed to vote openly for an unjust proposal or an unworthy candidate. But once the people became corrupt and votes were sold, secrecy was appropriate. Buyers could then be held back by mistrust, and scoundrels could accept money without having to betray their country.

I know Cicero condemns this change and blames it for part of the Republic's ruin. I recognise the weight his authority carries on this question, but cannot agree. On the contrary, I believe that failing to make enough such changes must hasten the State's destruction. A regimen suited to healthy people does not suit the sick. Likewise, we should not try to govern a corrupted people with the laws a good people needs. Nothing proves this better than Venice's long-lived Republic. Its shadow still survives solely because its laws suit only wicked men.

Citizens were therefore given tablets enabling each to vote without revealing his choice. New procedures also governed collecting the tablets, counting votes, comparing totals, etc. Yet all these precautions failed to prevent frequent suspicions about the honesty of the officials responsible.[2] Finally, edicts were issued to stop intrigue and the buying and selling of votes. Their sheer number shows how useless they were.

Near the Republic's end, extraordinary measures were often needed to make up for inadequate laws. Sometimes miracles were alleged, but although this could deceive the people, it could not deceive their rulers. Sometimes an assembly was summoned in haste before candidates could organise their factions. At other times talk filled an entire sitting, once it was clear that the people had been won over and were about to take the wrong side. Eventually ambition escaped every attempt made to restrain it. Most astonishing of all, amid these abuses this vast people, thanks to its ancient rules, continued to elect magistrates, enact laws, judge cases, and conduct both public and private business almost as readily as the senate itself could have done.

This applied when they assembled by centuries. In the other two forms, the people met in the _forum_ or elsewhere, and the _capite censi_ then possessed as much influence and authority as the leading citizens.

chapters.title: Book 4, Chapter 5 — The Tribunate
paragraphs: When the State's component parts cannot be brought into exact proportion, or when unavoidable causes keep altering their relationship, a special magistracy is established. It belongs to no corporate body formed by the other parts. Its task is to restore each part's proper relation to the rest, providing a connecting or intermediate term between prince and people, between prince and Sovereign, or, if necessary, between both pairs at once.

I shall call this body the _tribunate_. It preserves the laws and legislative power. Sometimes it shields the Sovereign from the government, as Rome's tribunes of the people did. Sometimes it supports government against the people, as Venice's Council of Ten does today. Sometimes it keeps the two in balance, as the Ephors did in Sparta.

The tribunate is not a component part of the city, and should share neither legislative nor executive power. Yet that very exclusion increases its own power: it can do nothing itself, but can prevent anything from being done. As guardian of the laws, it is more sacred and more revered than either the prince who carries them out or the Sovereign who enacts them. Rome showed this plainly. Proud patricians, despite their contempt for the people, had to bow before one of the people's officers, although he possessed neither auspices nor jurisdiction.

Properly moderated, the tribunate is the strongest support a sound constitution can possess. But if its power exceeds the proper measure even slightly, it overturns the entire State. Weakness, conversely, does not come naturally to it. As long as it has any existence, it is never weaker than it needs to be.

It turns tyrannical when it takes executive power instead of merely restraining it, or attempts to set aside the laws instead of merely protecting them. The Ephors' enormous power did no harm while Sparta retained her morals. Once corruption began, however, it accelerated the process. Agis's successor avenged his blood after these tyrants murdered him. Both the Ephors' crime and their punishment hastened the republic's destruction; after Cleomenes, Sparta ceased to matter. Rome died in the same way. The tribunes' excessive power, gradually seized for themselves, eventually protected the emperors who destroyed liberty--with the assistance of laws originally made to secure it. Venice's Council of Ten, meanwhile, is a tribunal of blood, dreaded by patricians and people alike. Far from nobly defending the laws, now that those laws have been degraded it does nothing but strike secret blows that no one dares acknowledge.

Like government, the tribunate loses strength as its membership increases. Rome's tribunes began with two members, then rose to five. When they wished to double that number, the senate permitted it, confident that one could be used to restrain another. Afterwards it made ample use of precisely that method.

The best safeguard against usurpation by so formidable a body would be to interrupt its existence instead of making it permanent. No government has yet tried this. The periods of suspension should be regulated and should never last long enough for abuses to become entrenched. The law could fix these intervals while allowing extraordinary commissions to shorten them readily whenever necessary.

I see no drawback to this method. As I have said, the tribunate forms no part of the constitution, so removing it leaves the constitution unaffected. It also seems effective: a magistrate whose office has just been restored begins with the powers the law grants him, rather than those his predecessor had come to exercise.

chapters.title: Book 4, Chapter 6 — The Dictatorship
paragraphs: Laws cannot readily bend to circumstances, and in certain cases this rigidity can make them disastrous, bringing the State to ruin in a crisis. The ordered, slow procedures they prescribe take time that circumstances do not always allow. A thousand situations may arise for which the legislator has made no provision. An essential part of foresight is recognising that no one can foresee everything.
It is therefore a mistake to make political institutions so rigid that their operation cannot be suspended. Even Sparta sometimes let its laws fall silent.

Only the gravest dangers, however, can outweigh the danger of changing the public order. The sacred authority of law should never be halted unless the country's existence is at risk. In these rare and unmistakable cases, a particular act secures public safety by entrusting it to the most worthy person. Depending on the danger's nature, this responsibility can be conferred in either of two ways.

If making government more active provides a sufficient remedy, power is concentrated in the hands of one or two of its members. In this case the change affects only the manner in which the laws are administered, not the authority of the laws themselves. If, however, the danger is such that the legal machinery obstructs the preservation of the laws, a supreme ruler is appointed to silence them all and briefly suspend sovereign authority. In such circumstances the general will is beyond doubt: the people's first wish is plainly that the State survive. Suspending legislative authority therefore does not abolish it. The magistrate who silences it has no power to make it speak. He rules over it, but cannot represent it. He may do anything except legislate.

Rome's senate used the first method when it instructed the consuls, in an established sacred formula, to safeguard the Republic. The second method appeared when one consul appointed a dictator,[1] a practice Rome had borrowed from Alba.

In the Republic's early years, dictators were appointed very frequently. The State was not yet secure enough to preserve itself through the strength of its constitution alone. The morals of that age made many precautions unnecessary that other times would have required. No one feared that a dictator would misuse his authority or retain it after his term. On the contrary, such great power seemed a burden to the man who held it, and he hurried to surrender it. It was as though standing in the place of the laws were too troublesome and dangerous a position to keep.

My objection to the careless use of this supreme magistracy in early times therefore concerns its loss of standing, rather than its abuse. When it was freely employed for elections, dedications and purely formal occasions, it risked becoming less formidable in an emergency. People might grow accustomed to treating as empty a title they saw used only for empty ceremonies.

By the Republic's end, the more cautious Romans were as unreasonably reluctant to appoint dictators as they had once been eager. Their fears were plainly groundless. The capital's weakness protected it from the magistrates within it. A dictator could sometimes defend public liberty, but could never endanger it. Rome's chains would be forged in her armies, not in Rome itself. The feeble resistance of Marius to Sulla, and of Pompey to Cæsar, clearly showed what authority inside the city could expect when confronted by force from outside.

This misunderstanding caused serious mistakes. One example was the failure to appoint a dictator during the Catilinarian conspiracy. Only the city itself, and at most some province in Italy, was involved. A dictator's legally unlimited authority would have allowed him to end the plot quickly. Instead, it was suppressed only through a combination of fortunate accidents that prudent men had no right to count on.

The senate instead merely handed all its power to the consuls. To act effectively, Cicero therefore had to exceed his authority on a matter of life and death. The first burst of joy brought approval of his conduct, but later he was rightly made to answer for citizens' blood shed against the law. No such accusation could have been made against a dictator. Yet the consul's eloquence prevailed. Roman though he was, he prized his own glory above his country. Rather than seek chiefly the safest and most lawful way to save the State, he wanted all the credit for saving it.[2] He was consequently honoured justly as Rome's liberator, and punished justly as a law-breaker. However splendid his recall, it was unquestionably a pardon.

However this great responsibility is granted, its term must be very short and incapable of extension. In the crises that call for it, the State is either quickly saved or quickly lost. Once the immediate need has passed, dictatorship becomes either tyrannical or useless. Roman dictators held office for only six months, and most resigned before their term ended. Had the term been longer, they might have sought to prolong it further, as the decemvirs did after being appointed for a year. The dictator had just enough time to meet the emergency that occasioned his appointment, and none to devise further projects.
There is something shameful about placing a man above the laws.
He did not dare appoint himself, and had no certainty that his colleague would choose him.

chapters.title: Book 4, Chapter 7 — The Censorship
paragraphs: Just as law declares the general will, censorship declares the public judgment. Public opinion is the law administered by the censor, who, like the prince, does no more than apply it to particular cases.
The censorial tribunal does not determine the people's opinion; it merely announces it. As soon as its judgment parts company with that opinion, its decisions have no validity.

There is no point separating a nation's morals from what it esteems. Both rest on the same principle and are necessarily inseparable. Everywhere, opinion rather than nature determines which pleasures a people chooses. Correct men's opinions and their morals will correct themselves. Men always love what is good, or what they consider good; their mistake lies in judging goodness. It is that judgment, therefore, that must be guided. To judge morals is to judge honour, and whoever judges honour takes opinion as his law.

A people's constitution shapes its opinions. Although law does not regulate morals directly, legislation brings them into being. When legislation weakens, morals decline. At that point the censors' judgment cannot accomplish what the force of law has failed to achieve.

Censorship can therefore help preserve morality, but can never restore it. Establish censors while the laws retain their strength. Once that strength is gone, hope is gone as well: no legitimate power can remain strong after the laws have lost their force.

Censorship sustains morals by keeping opinion from corruption, wisely applying it to preserve its soundness, and sometimes settling it while it is still uncertain. In France the use of seconds in duels had reached outrageous extremes. A royal edict ended it simply with these words: "As for those who are cowards enough to call upon seconds." This judgment anticipated the public's and immediately fixed it. But other edicts from the same source attempted to label duelling itself cowardice--which indeed it is. Common opinion did not see it that way. The public therefore ignored an official judgment on a matter about which it had already made up its mind.

Elsewhere[1] I have said that public opinion admits no coercion, so the tribunal representing it needs no trace of coercive power. We cannot admire enough the skill with which the Romans, and still more the Lacedæmonians, used this resource, which we moderns have entirely lost.

When a man of bad character offered a sound proposal to the Spartan Council, the Ephors ignored him and arranged for a virtuous citizen to make the same proposal. What honour for one and disgrace for the other, without praising or blaming either! Some drunkards from Samos[2] defiled the Ephors' tribunal. The following day a public edict granted Samians permission to be filthy. Actual punishment would have been less severe than this impunity. Once Sparta judges something right or wrong, Greece does not appeal against her decision.
I discussed this more fully in my _Letter to M. d'Alembert_.
I am forbidden to name them on this occasion.

chapters.title: Book 4, Chapter 8 — Civil Religion
paragraphs: Originally men recognised no kings except the gods and no form of government except theocracy. They reasoned as Caligula did, and in that age their reasoning was correct. Human feelings take a long time to change enough for men to accept their equals as masters in the hope of gaining something from submission.

Placing a God over each political society necessarily produced as many gods as there were peoples. Two peoples who were strangers and almost always enemies could not long acknowledge one master: two armies fighting each other could not obey one commander. Division into nations thus produced polytheism, which in turn produced theological and civil intolerance. As we shall see, these two kinds of intolerance are fundamentally the same.

The Greeks liked to discover their own gods among the barbarians because they regarded themselves as those peoples' natural Sovereigns. But nothing is more absurd than the scholarship of our own day that identifies and mixes up different nations' gods. As though Moloch, Saturn and Chronos were one god! As though the Phœnician Baal were identical with the Greek Zeus and the Latin Jupiter! As though imaginary beings bearing different names could have anything in common!

Why were there no religious wars in pagan times, when every State had its own cult and gods? Precisely because every State possessed both its own worship and its own government, I reply, and therefore made no distinction between its gods and its laws. Political war was already theological war. The gods' territories, so to speak, followed national boundaries. One people's god had no rights over another people. Pagan gods were not jealous: they divided the world's dominion among themselves. Even Moses and the Hebrews sometimes adopted this outlook when speaking of the God of Israel. They did indeed treat the Canaanites' gods as powerless: that proscribed people had been condemned to destruction, and they were to take its place. But remember how they spoke of the territories of neighbouring peoples whom they were forbidden to attack! "Is not the possession of what belongs to your god Chamos lawfully your due?" said Jephthah to the Ammonites. "We have the same title to the lands our conquering God has made his own."[1] To my mind, this acknowledges that Chamos's rights and those of the God of Israel are of the same kind.

Yet when the Jews, subjected first to Babylon's kings and later to Syria's, stubbornly refused to recognise any god but their own, their refusal was treated as rebellion against their conqueror. It brought upon them the persecutions recounted in their history, without parallel until Christianity appeared.[2]

Every religion was thus bound exclusively to the laws of the State prescribing it. A people could be converted only by being enslaved, and conquest was the only form of missionary work. Changing worship was a law imposed on the defeated, so victory had to come before anyone could demand the change. Men did not fight for the gods; the gods fought for men, as in Homer. Each man asked his god for victory and repaid him with new altars. Before capturing a city, the Romans called on its gods to leave. When they left the Tarentines their offended gods, they considered those gods subordinate to their own and obliged to pay homage. They allowed conquered peoples to retain their gods just as they retained their laws. Often the only tribute demanded was a wreath for the Jupiter of the Capitol.

Eventually the Romans spread their worship and gods along with their empire. They also frequently adopted the gods of conquered peoples, granting the rights of the city to both alike. Gradually, the peoples of this enormous empire found themselves surrounded by multitudes of gods and cults, almost identical everywhere. Paganism throughout the known world thus finally became a single religion.

These were the circumstances in which Jesus came to establish a spiritual kingdom on earth. By separating the theological system from the political, he ended the State's unity and introduced the internal divisions that have troubled Christian peoples ever since. Pagans could not have conceived the new idea of a kingdom in another world. They therefore always saw Christians as actual rebels who only pretended to submit, waiting for a chance to become independent and master their rulers. In their view, Christians meant to seize by cunning the authority they professed, in their weakness, to respect. This explains the persecutions.

The pagans' fears came true. Everything then changed its appearance. The humble Christians adopted a different language, and this supposed kingdom of another world soon became, under a visible head, the most violent earthly despotism.

But a prince and civil laws always continued to exist. This divided power and conflict of jurisdictions made sound political organisation impossible in Christian States. Men have never managed to establish whether their duty was to obey their ruler or their priest.

Several peoples, even in Europe and nearby, have unsuccessfully tried to preserve or restore the ancient system. Everywhere the spirit of Christianity has prevailed. Religious worship has either remained independent of the Sovereign or become independent again, with no necessary connection to the body of the State. Mahomet's views were very sound, and he bound his political system together well. As long as his successors, the caliphs, preserved his form of government, it really was united and, in that respect, good. But the Arabs became prosperous, learned, civilised, lax and cowardly, and barbarians conquered them. The split between the two powers reappeared. It is less conspicuous among Mahometans than Christians, but still exists, particularly in the sect of Ali. In States such as Persia its effects are continually felt.

Among our own peoples, England's Kings have made themselves heads of the Church, and the Czars have followed suit. Yet this title makes them its ministers more than its masters. What they chiefly acquire is the power to preserve it, rather than the right to change it: they are its princes, not its legislators. Wherever the clergy forms a corporate body,[3] it is master and legislator in its own country. England and Russia therefore have two powers, two Sovereigns, just as other countries do.

Of all Christian writers, only the philosopher Hobbes has recognised both the evil and its remedy. He dared to propose joining the eagle's two heads again, restoring everywhere the political unity without which no State or government can be properly constituted. Yet he should have recognised that Christianity's domineering spirit cannot coexist with his system, and that priestly interests would always outweigh the State's. His political theory has attracted hatred less for what is false and terrible in it than for what is just and true.[4]

I believe a study of history from this perspective would readily refute the opposing opinions of Bayle and Warburton. The first denies that religion can benefit the body politic at all; the second calls Christianity its strongest support. We could show the former that no State has ever been founded without religion, and the latter that Christian law ultimately harms the State's constitution more by weakening it than it helps by strengthening it. To make my meaning clear, I need only give greater precision to the excessively vague ideas about religion in relation to this subject.

Religion considered in relation to society, whether society in general or a particular society, can likewise be divided into two kinds: the religion of man and the religion of the citizen. The first has no temples, altars or ceremonies. It consists solely of inward worship of the supreme God and the eternal duties of morality. This is the Gospel's religion, pure and simple: true theism, which we may call natural divine right or law. The second is established within one country. It supplies that country with its gods and protecting patrons, its doctrines, ceremonies and public worship, all prescribed by law. Beyond the one nation practising it, it sees only unbelievers, foreigners and barbarians. For it, human rights and duties reach no farther than its own altars. All early peoples had religions of this kind, which we may call civil or positive divine right or law.

A third, more peculiar religion gives men two sets of laws, two rulers and two countries. It subjects them to conflicting duties and makes loyalty to both religion and citizenship impossible. Such are the religions of the Lamas and the Japanese, and Roman Christianity, which may be called the religion of the priest. It creates a kind of mixed, anti-social code for which there is no name.

Politically, all three kinds of religion have defects. The third is so obviously bad that stopping to demonstrate it would waste time. Whatever destroys social unity is worthless; any institution that puts man in conflict with himself is worthless.

The second kind is good because it joins divine worship to love of the laws. It makes the country an object of the citizens' adoration, teaching them that service to the State is service to its protecting god. This is a theocracy: the prince alone can be pontiff, and the magistrates alone can be priests. Dying for the country becomes martyrdom, breaking its laws becomes impiety, and subjecting an offender to public condemnation delivers him to the gods' anger: _Sacer estod_.

Yet it is bad because its foundation in falsehood and error deceives men, makes them gullible and superstitious, and buries true worship of the Divinity beneath empty ceremony. It is also bad when it grows tyrannical and exclusive, making a people bloodthirsty and intolerant. Such a people breathes fire and slaughter, treating the killing of anyone who disbelieves in its gods as a sacred deed. It thereby places itself in a natural state of war against all other peoples, gravely endangering its own security.

That leaves the religion of man, or Christianity--not today's Christianity, but the Gospel's, which is quite different. Through this holy, sublime and true religion, all men recognise one another as brothers, children of a single God. The society joining them together survives even death.

But this religion has no special connection to the body politic. It leaves laws with whatever force they possess on their own, adding nothing to it. One of the great bonds that can unite a particular society therefore remains inactive. Worse still, instead of attaching citizens' hearts to the State, it draws them away from everything earthly. I know nothing more opposed to the spirit of society.

We are told that true Christians would make the most perfect society imaginable. I see only one great difficulty with this supposition: a society of true Christians would not be a society of human beings.
