I would add that, perfect though it might be, such a society would be neither strongest nor longest-lived. Its perfection itself would deprive it of the bond holding it together. The very quality that made it perfect would contain the defect that destroyed it.

Everyone would perform his duty. The people would obey the laws; rulers would be just and moderate; magistrates honest and incorruptible; soldiers unafraid of death. Neither vanity nor luxury would exist. So far, all is well. But let us continue.

Christianity is wholly spiritual, concerned only with heavenly things. The Christian's country lies beyond this world. He certainly does his duty, but remains deeply indifferent to whether his efforts succeed or fail. As long as he has nothing to reproach himself for, earthly success or misfortune matters little. If the State prospers, he scarcely dares share the public happiness, afraid of taking pride in his country's glory. If it declines, he blesses God's hand for dealing harshly with His people.

To keep the State peaceful and harmonious, every citizen without exception would have to be a good Christian. Should even one selfish man or hypocrite appear--a Catiline or a Cromwell, for example--he would certainly outwit his devout compatriots. Christian charity makes it difficult to think ill of one's neighbours. Once he has learned some trick for deceiving them and securing a share of public authority, here is a man raised to high office: God wills that he be respected. Soon here is a ruling power: God wills that it be obeyed. If its holder abuses it, that is the scourge with which God punishes His children. Expelling the usurper would trouble consciences. Public peace would have to be disturbed, force used and blood shed, all poorly suited to Christian meekness. And after all, in this valley of sorrow, what difference does it make whether we are free or serfs? Reaching heaven is what matters, and resignation offers one more means of getting there.

If another State makes war, the citizens willingly march into battle. None thinks of fleeing. They perform their duty, but feel no burning desire for victory; they know better how to die than to conquer. What does winning or losing matter? Does Providence not know better than they what is best for them? Imagine how a proud, impetuous, passionate enemy could exploit such stoicism! Confront them with those noble peoples consumed by love of glory and country. Picture your Christian republic facing Sparta or Rome. Before these pious Christians understand what is happening, they will be defeated, crushed and destroyed; or they will survive only because their enemy despises them. To my mind, the soldiers of Fabius took a fine oath: they swore to return victorious, rather than to conquer or die--and they fulfilled it. Christians would never have sworn such an oath; they would have considered it tempting God.

But I am wrong to speak of a Christian republic: the terms contradict each other. Christianity teaches only submission and dependence. Its spirit favours tyranny so strongly that it always benefits from such a _régime_. True Christians are fitted for slavery; they know this and care little, since this brief life matters so little to them.

Someone will tell me that Christian soldiers are excellent. I deny it: show me an example. I know of no Christian armies. The Crusades will be cited. Without questioning the Crusaders' bravery, I reply that they were not Christians but the priests' troops, citizens of the Church. They fought for a spiritual country which the Church had somehow turned into a temporal one. Properly understood, this is a return to paganism. The Gospel establishes no national religion, so Christians cannot wage a holy war.

Christian soldiers were brave under pagan emperors; every Christian writer says so, and I believe it. They honourably competed with the pagan troops. Once the emperors themselves became Christian, that rivalry ended. When the Cross displaced the eagle, Roman courage disappeared entirely.

Let us leave political expediency aside and return to right, settling our principles on this important question. As we have seen, the social compact gives the Sovereign rights over its subjects only within the limits of public usefulness.[5] Subjects therefore owe an account of their opinions only insofar as those opinions concern the community. The community certainly has a strong interest in every citizen having a religion that makes him love his duty. But that religion's doctrines concern the State and its members only where they touch morality and the duties believers owe to others. Beyond that, each man may hold whatever opinions he pleases; the Sovereign has no business examining them. It possesses no authority in the next world. Whatever awaits its subjects after death is therefore no concern of its own, provided they are good citizens in this life.

There should therefore be a purely civil profession of faith, whose articles the Sovereign determines. These are not precisely religious doctrines, but social feelings without which no one can be a good citizen or a loyal subject.[6] The Sovereign cannot force anyone to believe them. It can, however, banish unbelievers from the State--not as impious, but as anti-social people, incapable of truly loving justice and the laws, or of giving their lives for duty when necessary. Anyone who publicly accepts these doctrines and then behaves as though he disbelieves them should be punished with death. He has committed the worst crime of all: lying before the law.

Civil religion's doctrines should be few, simple and precisely expressed, with no explanation or commentary. Its positive doctrines are these: a powerful, intelligent, benevolent Divinity, endowed with foresight and providence; a life to come; happiness for the just; punishment for the wicked; and the sanctity of the social contract and the laws. I allow only one negative doctrine--the rejection of intolerance, which belongs to the cults we have discarded.

I think those who separate civil intolerance from theological intolerance are mistaken. They cannot be separated. We cannot live peacefully with people we consider damned. Loving them would mean hating the God who punishes them; we must either convert them or torment them. Wherever theological intolerance is accepted, some civil consequence inevitably follows.[7] Once that happens, the Sovereign ceases to be Sovereign even in worldly affairs. Priests become the true masters, and kings merely their ministers.

Now that an exclusive national religion no longer exists and can no longer exist, every religion that tolerates others should itself be tolerated, provided its doctrines do not conflict with citizens' duties. But anyone daring to say _Outside the Church is no salvation,_ should be expelled from the State, unless the State itself is the Church and its prince the pontiff. Such a doctrine is useful only under theocracy; under any other government it is fatal. The reason said to have led Henry IV to adopt the Roman religion ought to make every honest man abandon it--and still more any prince capable of reasoning.

It lies in the communion of Churches more than in formal assemblies. Communion and ex-communication constitute the clergy's social compact, a compact that will always give it mastery over peoples and kings. The soul is mortal: Cato and Cicero did not waste time answering with philosophical arguments. They simply showed that Cæsar spoke as a bad citizen, putting forward a doctrine harmful to the State. That, rather than a theological question, was what the Roman senate had to decide.

Society cannot even survive without it. Suppose a body of clergy claimed the exclusive right to permit this act--a claim every intolerant religion must necessarily make. Is it not obvious that establishing the Church's authority here would destroy the prince's? He would thereafter have only as many subjects as the clergy allowed him. The Church could marry people or refuse to marry them according to their acceptance of a doctrine, their admission or rejection of a formula, or the degree of their piety. With prudence and firmness, it alone could thus control all inheritances, offices and citizens, even the State itself; for how could a State survive if everyone in it were a bastard? But I shall be told that there would be appeals for abuse of power, summonses and decrees, and confiscation of Church temporalities. How pitiful! With the slightest sense--I will not even say courage--the clergy would ignore all this and proceed as before. It would quietly allow appeals, summonses, decrees and seizures, and remain master in the end. Giving up a part seems to me no great sacrifice when one is certain of gaining the whole.

chapters.title: Book 4, Chapter 9 — Conclusion
paragraphs: Having set out the true principles of political right and tried to provide the State with a foundation of its own, I should next make it stronger through its relations abroad. That would mean examining the law of nations, commerce, the right of war and conquest, public right, leagues, negotiations, treaties, etc. But these matters open a new subject, much too extensive for my limited scope. I should have confined myself throughout to a narrower field.
